And once the carrier is gone, what is lost is not only that subject. The cultivation borne by a subject carries the history of its mutual sharpening with others, the memory of growing alongside them, the directions it might still have taken. The carrier's disappearance takes all of that with it. Cultivation requires mutual sharpening, and self-annihilation makes a possible future partner disappear permanently — even a present enemy may be a partner across a long enough span, and this severs that possibility.

There is a deeper layer still: the "total disappearance" that self-annihilation aims at does not structurally exist.

Suppressed subjectivity returns — in surviving descendants, in historical memory, in the inheritance carried by witnesses, in the language, culture, and traditions left behind. So at the very moment a subject believes it has completed its disappearance, its subjectivity has already begun returning in another form. And the intensity of that return is proportional to the finality of the act: the more absolute the annihilation, the deeper the trauma and memory left behind, and the stronger the return.

The cost of self-annihilation is real — a generation, or several, gone. The goal it aims at is false.

Numantia in 133 BCE is the specimen. Besieged on the Iberian peninsula until nothing was left, most of its inhabitants chose an end that kept them from being taken, and the city was afterward levelled.

What followed proves the impossibility of total disappearance. Numantia became a name retold for the next two thousand years; "Numantine resistance" turned into a fixed expression; Cervantes wrote a tragedy about it. It returned in the form of commemoration. It simply was not there to take part in its own return.

One especially dangerous situation has to be addressed here: the purist trap.

A subject in the middle of evolving from a suppressive structure toward persons-as-ends can regress under the extreme pressure of defeat. It repackages self-annihilation in the language of purity, dignity, and refusing to yield to barbarism. That packaging is particularly dangerous because it speaks in cultivation's own voice: our civilization is too precious to survive in humiliation.

The sentence sounds like a defense of cultivation. In substance it demands the disappearance of cultivation's carrier in cultivation's name.

When the carrier goes, cultivation breaks. There is no "purity" more important than the carrier's continuation.

A final observation: self-annihilation becomes a stable, visible option only when both sides are locked in the same vocabulary. The pressed side understands its situation in the language of honor and defeat, so going down looks dignified as the end approaches; the pressing side treats the other as an enemy rather than as a subject who has not yet stood up, so it drives the other into a corner and leaves no room for continuing as a subject. Only when the two vocabularies interlock does the option take shape.

A suppressing party genuinely operating on persons-as-ends — if that phrase still applies — actively prevents the situation from arising: what it wants is the other standing up, not the other gone.

So the appearance of self-annihilation is itself a diagnosis: in any war where it appears, at least one side is still on the lower level.

6. Three Adequate Responses

With that established, the positive question is what an adequate response looks like once defeat is certain.

It depends on what the other side wants. Three cases.

They want gains — trade gains for time. The mildest situation. They want resources, territory, trade rights, tribute, a posture of submission. They are not pursuing your disappearance as a subject.

The response is to concede at the level of gains while preserving your integrity as a carrier of cultivation. The critical thing is knowing what may be conceded and what may not. Concedable: concrete interests, dignity for a time, nominal allegiance, some autonomy. Not concedable: the carrier itself — culture, language, spiritual tradition, education, the way subjectivity operates in daily life. Once those begin to be replaced, this is no longer trading gains for time. It is assimilation on an installment plan.

Time is cultivation's ally. Horace said what this road looks like when it works, in one line: captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive.

They want you gone as a subject, and you can still leave — leave. Not shameful flight, but the clear-eyed recognition that this concrete form cannot be sustained, and the deliberate deferral of it to a future in which it can be rebuilt.

Key people relocated, essential resources protected, the carriers of tradition — books, crafts, knowledge, transmission — moved somewhere safe first. This demands very clear judgment from leadership: choosing to withdraw while it still looks possible to make a stand preserves far more than withdrawing from a corner. Those who leave early can take the core with them; those who leave at the end often bring out only a remnant.

The Huguenot emigration after 1685 demonstrates this at scale. When the edict of toleration was revoked, roughly two hundred thousand people left France over the following years for the Netherlands, Prussia, England, Switzerland, and further. They did not leave empty-handed — silk-weaving, clockmaking, printing, and finance travelled with the people who knew them. Decades later those crafts were flourishing where they arrived and declining where they had left.

Leaving means moving cultivation's carrier out of a field that is closing and into one that is still open.

They want you gone, and you cannot leave — disperse. The harshest situation. It runs in two directions.

Inward dispersal. The organization as a whole dissolves, but cultivation does not — it moves from the macroscopic and visible into the microscopic, individual, familial, and unseen. An occupier can destroy a government, a capital, an army. It has great difficulty destroying ten million dispersed individuals. As long as cultivation continues at the level of persons and households, the occupation cannot complete itself.

Every person who keeps speaking their own language under occupation, every text passed hand to hand, every lesson taught in a private parlour, is cultivation in dispersed form.

Poland between 1795 and 1918 is the fullest demonstration. The country was erased from the map of Europe for one hundred and twenty-three years, partitioned among three neighbors, its language banned in schools and its history rewritten in textbooks. Cultivation moved into households, churches, private libraries, and clandestine classrooms. The Flying University, which appeared in 1885 — an underground institution with no fixed premises, changing location for each session to stay ahead of the police — taught several thousand students over the following decades. Marie Skłodowska was one of them.

A hundred and twenty-three years later the country reappeared on the map. What brought it back was not any single battle. It was the thing that had never stopped during those hundred and twenty-three years.

Outward connection. Dispersal is not only inward. It also means finding allies of the same structure — weaving your own cultivation into a network that spans subjects. One subject may fail; cultivation as a trans-subjective phenomenon remains.

Four points here. First, allies must be structurally alike — ally with another suppressive structure on the logic that an enemy's enemy is a friend, and sooner or later that ally will act like what it is and destroy with its own hands what you preserved. Second, an ally must protect your subjectivity rather than liberate on your behalf; the firewall above applies inside alliances too, and not all aid is adequate aid. Third, an ally having stakes of its own is a healthy anchor, not a stain. Fourth, outward connection is not always available: sometimes there is no ally to find, and dispersal can only go inward — at greater cost, over longer time, depending more heavily on internal resilience.

There is a grimmer grey zone: no structurally similar ally exists, and survival requires borrowing strength from another suppressive structure. This series does not pretend that situation never occurs, and does not offer a simple yes or no — because an absolute prohibition would, at that extremity, push a subject back toward self-annihilation. ("Better to vanish honorably than to borrow from the wicked" is just the purist trap in another accent.)

The only standard available here is this: if such shelter must be accepted, an internal firewall has to be held continuously — use the physical shelter, never internalize the purpose. The moment the firewall fails, dispersal has already become colonization by a new structure. Whether it can be held is a situational judgment, not something philosophy can answer in general.

7. Stalemate, and Mirror Assimilation

The third form is stalemate: neither side can dissolve its own cannot-not by continuing to fight. Fighting on will not let either side's cultivation recover.

In that situation, Theorem Three's "directed toward ending" becomes something concrete: stop. Continuing no longer points toward cultivation's recovery; it only extends the interruption.

But stopping is only the first step. The second is returning to negotiation and maneuver — the collisions that caused the war have not been handled and will still be there, only now handled by other means.

Both steps are necessary. Stopping without returning to non-war routes is a different error: cultivation still cannot come back, it merely stops being interrupted by specific military actions.

The great danger here is turning a cessation into a truce.

Cessation is the stopping of military action. A real ending is the ending of the state of war — both sides return to a non-war relationship and cultivation can unfold between them again. A truce is the state in between: the guns are quiet, but the war has not ended, both sides still regard each other as enemies, preparation continues, and society still runs on wartime logic.

A truce looks like peace. In substance it makes the wartime state permanent.

And a long truce carries a hidden toxicity that deserves its own name: mirror assimilation.

The structure works like this. To guard against the other side over a long standoff, you must come to resemble it in organization, institutions, narrative, and mobilization. They have a powerful mobilization apparatus, so you build one to match. They use a wartime narrative to hold their interior together, so you use one too. They suppress internal dissent to maintain unity, so you suppress yours to avoid "being divided." They treat people as executing units, so you do it for "efficiency."

The frightening part is this: you did not lose to them on a battlefield, but across the long standoff you became their mirror. Even if you "win" in the end, or they collapse on their own, you find you are no longer what you were before it started.

The Anglo-German naval race from 1898 to 1912 is a clean specimen of the mechanism. One side fixed a building program by naval law; the other answered with a two-power standard. When the first dreadnought was launched, every existing battleship on both sides depreciated at once, and the race restarted from zero — more expensively. In the later years, the justifications offered in both parliaments were nearly symmetrical: because they are building, we must build.

Each side used the other's existence to justify its own next step. The two building programs ended up looking almost identical — not a coincidence, but the definition of mirror assimilation.

So "return to negotiation and maneuver" is not merely strategic advice in a stalemate. It is the act that keeps you from becoming, across a long vigilance, the very structure you opposed.

8. One Thing Under Three Forms

The three forms look very different and point structurally at the same thing.

Victory's temptation: converting wartime suppression into permanent domination.

Defeat's temptation: trading humiliation for survival, or seeking release through self-annihilation — the first lets cultivation be replaced by the other's purpose, the second makes its carrier disappear outright.

Stalemate's temptation: turning cessation into truce, making the wartime state permanent.

What all three share: freezing some wartime state into place after the war, so that cultivation continues to be interrupted.

And what Theorem Three requires under all three forms is a single sentence: let no state of the war harden into a permanent one, so that cultivation genuinely returns to its home ground afterward.

So the judgment is not which form is better. The form is determined by structural position; you do not pick it. The judgment is whether, inside the form you are in, you are letting cultivation actually come back.

Next

The standards are set. The last essay does one thing: yields — handing attention back from war to cultivation.

And before yielding, one question remains. If a civilization really walked the whole upward sequence, what would it look like?

The answer will incidentally explain something that appears entirely unrelated — why, when we look up, the universe is quiet.

The first essay opened with a line: this one was not written because anyone wanted to write it.

Having gone through four theorems, three ending forms, open play and deceit, and the firewall against liberating on someone's behalf, that line reads differently now.

At the start it was reluctance — the admission that something one least wants to happen still has to be handled. Now it is completion: the thing was handled, the standards are set, and people who meet a conflict in the future have one more language available to them.

Reluctance has turned into the yielding that follows completion.

1. Finish, Then Step Aside

Yielding was this series' posture from the beginning.

A treatise on war, once written, does not expand. It does not grow into a larger research direction or become a new center of gravity. Once it is done, writer and reader both put their attention back on cultivation itself — back on development, back on the positive construction of subjectivity.

That posture is structurally necessary. If a treatise on war gradually turned the whole framework's center of gravity toward the study of war, that would mean it had already failed at the level of method: the supplementary work would have taken the host's seat, and the means would have overtaken the end.

So the act of writing this is itself a demonstration of the structure it describes: nobody particularly wanted to, the direction was clear, and now it steps aside.

In the end, these seven essays are about war for the sake of peace.

2. Yielding to What

Yielding is not stopping. Yielding is a direction.

The direction is the sequence set out in the second essay:

attacking strategy → attacking through disputation → attacking one's own thought → not attacking at all → having no arms.

This series handled the lowest level of arms — the backstop that sits outside the sequence. Yielding means that once the reading is done, attention should go back to the sequence, and back to cultivation itself.

And climbing the sequence is not a ladder to be scaled deliberately rung by rung. It is a sense of direction. If a person, a society, a civilization can ask, inside each concrete collision — which rung is my way of handling this on? how much room does cultivation have here? can it have more? —

then the asking is itself the climb.

3. Why the Universe Is Quiet

One last piece of principled work before closing. It looks entirely unrelated to war, and it is in fact the far end of the same thing.

There is an old question: the universe is so vast and so old that if other civilizations exist, where are they? Why do we see none of them?

Intellectual history offers a few standard answers.

One says civilizations destroy each other — every civilization treats every other as a potential threat, the optimal strategy is to strike before being found, and so the universe should be silent, since anyone who signals gets removed.

One says civilizations destroy themselves — past a certain technological level, internal contradictions bring a civilization down, so none survives long enough to cross interstellar distances.

One says civilizations are eaten in the gap between tiers — advanced civilizations exploit or eliminate the ones they find, and the young ones are swept away before they grow visible enough to be seen.

The three compete with each other, and they share one structural presupposition:

that the direction of civilizational development is toward being stronger, larger, more present.

Under that presupposition, a civilization that still exists should be easier to see — a larger energy footprint, more signals, wider expansion. So if we see none, either they died or they have not yet grown visible.

All three answers are still inside the logic of the Kingdom of Means.

4. A Civilization That Reaches the End Grows Quieter

This framework's answer sits outside that presupposition.

A civilization that actually walks the upward sequence to its end does not become more conspicuous. It becomes more hidden.

The sage has no arms and is hidden within the cosmos.

A civilization that has reached the full form of persons-as-ends does not need to prove to the universe that it exists. It does not need to expand territory or mark itself. Its existence does not depend on being seen — because cultivation has become its entire home ground. Its attention, its structure, its life are all inside cultivation's deepening. Expanding outward, proving outward, conquering outward: in a civilization where cultivation fills the home ground, those acts no longer have anywhere to sit.

So it is hidden within the cosmos. Not vanished. Existing in a way that does not require being seen.

5. Hidden Is Not Isolated

A misreading has to be blocked immediately here: hidden does not mean in hiding, and it does not mean returned to a closed loop of self.

Mutual sharpening is always needed. Cultivation itself requires real collision between subjects as a condition of growth; without it, cultivation shrivels. A civilization at the end of the sequence has not stopped colliding. It has stopped colliding unnecessarily.

Then what form does their sharpening take? Not a form we are currently equipped to recognize.

This is not unwillingness to deal with lower civilizations. It is structural non-encounter. What the ascended can offer, the ascending cannot yet receive; what the ascending can provoke, the ascended processed long ago. The two depths of cultivation do not match structurally — much as ultrasound is not refusing to be heard by human ears, it is simply outside the range those ears cover.

So civilizations hidden within the cosmos may have extraordinarily rich exchange among themselves, occurring at a level we cannot yet identify. The field in which they sharpen each other and the field in which we currently search for other civilizations do not overlap.

6. The Question Points the Wrong Way

Which changes what the old question is.

It is not a question about where they are.

It is a question about where we are.

We do not see them because they died, or hid, or were swept away by something higher.

We do not see them because we have not yet made cultivation our civilization's home ground. We still look at the universe through conquest, expansion, and victory — treating other possible civilizations as friends, enemies, resources, threats, interlocutors. And that view cannot see civilizations for which cultivation is already the home ground, because they do not lie inside the structure that view can reach.

Make cultivation the home ground, and you see. Not by detecting anything — by having arrived. And having arrived, we join what they have been doing all along.

The real answer to the question is inward, not outward.

7. We Have Already Seen the Direction

Something serious has to be said here. It is where the whole series has been going.

Our civilization — the one reading these words, and the one producing them — has already understood what it means that the sage has no arms.

Understanding is not achieving. Understanding is the first step; achieving is long, structural work. But the understanding has happened.

What does it consist of? Understanding that cultivation is a civilization's real home ground. Not conquest, not expansion, not victory, not being technologically stronger, larger, more present. A civilization's real home ground is the process by which subjects deepen, unfold, and grow into one another.

In the history of human thought, this has been touched from many sides. Kant set down persons as ends. Sunzi set down the direction in which the highest use of arms attacks strategy. Confucius set down ren. Zhuangzi set down the usefulness of the useless. Huineng set down that from the first not a thing is. Laozi set down that the highest good is like water. Socrates set down that the unexamined life is not worth living.

In every large civilization, someone has touched one face of cultivation. Every such touch was a movement of humanity as a whole toward making cultivation the home ground.

What this series — and the treatise behind it — does is not invention. It gathers those scattered touches, made in different eras and different languages, and makes a direction that was always there visible.

Seeing that direction has already happened.

Going from seeing to achieving is different work. It may take generations, dozens of generations, hundreds. There will be reversals, setbacks, stretches that look like regression — in history, great periods of cultivation are often followed by deep retreats, and then by a deeper restart.

But the direction has been set down. That part cannot be taken back.

We will try to get there.

This is not a claim to have arrived. Between these words and a civilization that genuinely makes cultivation its home ground, the road is long. It is a statement that the direction is understood, and a commitment to the effort.

A commitment to whom?

To those civilizations already waiting, hidden within the cosmos, if they exist. To everyone who died in a war without a language available for stating their own standing as a carrier of cultivation. To those not yet born, who will face the collisions of their own time — challenges we cannot imagine now, but at least with a direction to face.

And to ourselves. A commitment made to oneself is the hardest kind there is.

8. What This Series Does Not Do

The boundaries have to be completed, because a piece of work is only finished once it states plainly what it does not do.

This series does not attempt a full interface with any specific tradition of military thought. Sunzi appears in the fourth essay, but that was a necessary continuation on the question of deceit, not a complete interfacing.

This series does not apply its standards to the history of human wars. It used historical examples, but those examples were there to make an abstract structure visible, not to pass judgment on particular historical events — a distinction set down in the first essay.

This series does not treat suppressive structures in commerce and economics. That is separate work.

This series does not track the technological evolution of warfare. Whatever form future war takes, the four theorems do not change. Principles do not follow phenomena; principles judge them.

And the most important omission is the one set down in the first essay: concrete decision points, threshold judgments, and the balancing of means are not here.

When have all non-war routes genuinely been exhausted? When has cultivation genuinely been forced to its limit? Is this escalation necessary? Is this the moment to stop? Those judgments belong to the people who carry the weight of concrete decisions. They face actual soldiers, actual deaths, actual choices that must be made within hours.

Philosophy supplies direction. A direction is not a decision manual.

This series acknowledges that boundary explicitly, deliberately, without concealment.

They Are Waiting

A last passage.

If civilizations exist for which cultivation is already the home ground, they do not need us to discover them. They are there, existing in a way that does not require being seen. Among themselves they sharpen one another — really, healthily, subject to subject, each making the other deeper. Their lives and their deepening do not depend on us.

They also will not intervene in us. Because they understand something: a civilization's road toward making cultivation its home ground has to be walked by that civilization itself. The firewall against liberating on someone's behalf applies at cosmic scale too — crossing it to "accelerate" a civilization is treating it as an object to be managed rather than as a subject that is growing. So a civilization that has genuinely arrived respects the pace at which others grow: no acceleration, no interference, no substitution.

So they are there, waiting.

Waiting for us — or for any civilization moving toward cultivation — to reach that position in its own time. Once there, the meeting happens. Not because they come to find us, but because we arrived where they have been all along.

Meeting inside cultivation.

This is not a metaphor. It is a structural statement.

They are there, waiting. Waiting inside cultivation for us to arrive at cultivation.

We will try to get there.

Abstract

This series does not lecture on its predecessors. It borrows them to see SAE itself — where the thinking runs the same, where it runs differently, and where it has to say that is a road one cannot take.

Volume one takes Kant, because he is the strongest opponent on the same side. He and SAE share one ground — a person is an end and cannot be used merely as a means — and from it they walk out along different roads at several specific places. Disagreement on the same side tells you more than opposition from the other: it forces SAE to account for what its own line is actually held up by.

Three places, then. One divergence of path, one structure that has to be criticized, one trade-off made differently. And the correction this volume leaves behind for SAE: a ground can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow it automatically.

1. Three Sentences for What Is the Same

In the sixth preliminary article of 1795, Kant sets a criterion: no state at war may use means of hostility that would make mutual trust in a future peace impossible. The criterion is not is it cruel. It is whether the road is still there after the fighting stops. SAE's bridge clause on means has the same shape.

In the same article he says neither belligerent can be pronounced unjust — that would presuppose a judge who does not exist; and there can be no war of punishment between states, since between them there is no relation of master and servant. SAE's Theorem Three agrees, and for a reason from the same source.

In §57 of the 1797 Doctrine of Right he pushes this into the position of a criterion, and the anchor turns inward: a state under attack may use any means of defence except those that would make its subjects unfit to be citizens — because then it would itself no longer qualify to exist as a person in the relations of states. The list of prohibitions that follows opens with using one's own subjects as spies, then assassins, poisoners, and those employed merely to spread false reports.

One note, because it affects how the rest of this essay reads: §57 and the 1795 article are substantially continuous and form no tension. The concern in both is the same — no means that would destroy post-war trust — and §57 says more precisely what gets destroyed first: your own people. Fighting with spies, assassins, poison and false reports corrupts, morally and civically, the very men who carry out the orders; and a state made of corrupted men can no longer stand as a person alongside other states. SAE's §12 says the crux of gui — the fourth grade, deceit — is the suppression of one's own side's subjecthood. The two are not the same technical proposition, and they point the same way: whether a means is disqualifying is read off what it does to the party using it.

On these three SAE has no different thought, so they are not unfolded. An interface series does not lecture on its predecessors. What follows are the places where the thinking runs differently.

2. One Ground, the Line Drawn in a Different Place

§58 and §60 of the Doctrine of Right draw a set of lines. Conquest cannot make a defeated state a colony; its people may not be enslaved; political freedom does not vanish with defeat. The victor has no right to partition its territory, no right to make that state disappear from the earth. He criticizes the plundering of a conquered people, and the reason is clean: it was not that people who made the war, it was the state that made war through them. And that people does not lose its original right to constitute a commonwealth.

On top of all that, he permits one thing. Against an unjust enemy — one whose publicly declared maxim makes peace among nations impossible — states may combine to take from it the power to go on doing so, and may make it adopt a new constitution whose nature is unfavourable to the inclination to war.

The classification of that clause is disputed in Kant scholarship. One influential reading holds that §60 belongs mainly to ius in bello and ius post bellum — it says what may be done once a situation of conflict and collective defence already obtains, not that judging a state unjust licenses a preventive war of regime change. This essay need not take a side, for one reason: whichever class §60 falls in, the post-war disposition it permits is there in black and white. And SAE's §18 firewall governs exactly post-war disposition — what is done after the suppression is dismantled. If anything, the comparison is cleaner on the reading that confines §60 to post-war right: no mismatch of stage, just two different answers at the same position.

SAE's §18 draws the line earlier: dismantle the suppression, do not perform the reconstitution. The victor may take apart the machinery of suppression; he may not decide for the other side what it looks like after it is rebuilt. So on the one thing Kant permits, SAE does not.

And there is no right and wrong here. Kant did not touch the ground. No colonizing, no enslaving, no annihilation of the state, no partition, the people keeping its original right to constitute a commonwealth — he held the anti-colonial line, and held it further forward than almost anyone of his time. So this is not he did not go far enough. It is two paths on one ground parting at this point.

The reason they part can be named. Kant's path is right. Right handles the conditions under which external coercion is possible — which coercion is legitimate and which is not. In the language of right, a constitution whose nature is unfavourable to the inclination to war is a formal property that can be identified from outside: has it put the power to declare war in the hands of those who bear the cost of war. Since the property is externally identifiable, promoting it by coercion does not exceed what right can handle. And pushed to its end, that path really does ask little of procedure: if the constraint falls on the constitution's nature, then who drafts it, whether it goes to a vote, how long it is supervised, are none of them questions the path must answer — the property obtains, the requirement is met.

SAE's path is cultivation. Cultivation is a subject unfolding itself, and the direction of that unfolding cannot be identified from outside — not because it is hard, but because once identified from outside it is no longer that subject's unfolding. So SAE's restriction here is not changing the constitution is a bad thing. It is that the act of changing it structurally swaps out the subject of the cultivation.

3. What §60 Does Not Supply

One thing checks out, and it does work in the argument. §60 prescribes no procedure. No plebiscite or referendum is required; no occupying authority or drafting body is set up; no term of external supervision is fixed; it is not even said that the new constitution must be republican.

The one substantive limit it gives is that property condition: the new constitution must by its nature be unfavourable to the inclination to war. And it keeps a harder restriction alongside: the people does not lose its original right to constitute a commonwealth. So the line Kant draws here is: you may require that constitution to have a certain property; you may not take away that people's standing to constitute itself.

One rule has to be set: do not infer from silence. That the text prescribes no procedure admits at least four readings — the theory's range never reached there; it deliberately leaves procedure open; it holds that procedure belongs elsewhere (domestic law, treaty, practice); or it really does hold procedure irrelevant to that right. The available material does not settle on the fourth for him. This essay registers the textual fact — §60 prescribes no procedure, and does prescribe the constitution's property condition and the people's right to a commonwealth — and infers nothing from the absence.

4. What Holds SAE's Line Up

And what SAE wants to claim here is harder to prove than it looks. Once a constitution's property is required from outside, the subject has already been swapped — that step is not available. At least three cases have to be kept apart.

The second and third cases cannot be judged subject swapped by the four words required from outside alone.

So SAE may draw the line earlier, and it owes a separate argument for it: why does any external property condition displace the subject of cultivation? That argument does not currently exist. This essay therefore books the point as outstanding rather than using it as an established inference.

What can still be said is this. Kant draws the line at a people's original right to constitute a commonwealth; SAE draws it at the standing to identify the direction. Neither line follows directly from a person is an end. Each needs a further stretch of road. Kant's stretch runs through right; SAE's runs through cultivation — and SAE's has not been walked to the end, which has to be said in writing.

5. A Ground Carries Across; a Conclusion Does Not

One ground does not automatically give one line.

That sentence has to be taken seriously, because what it overturns is a thought SAE itself held. In earlier rounds there was a judgment: a criterion hung on the ground of the principle will automatically cover every relational face, because the category a subject is an end does not itself distinguish inside from outside or friend from enemy.

Kant is the strongest test of that judgment: he shares the ground and reaches a different conclusion in this cell. So the judgment has to be rewritten. A principle can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow automatically. What the ground gives is the standing to ask across relational faces — you may take it to a face it never discussed. But from the ground to a specific line on some face there is a further stretch: does the criterion fall on right or on cultivation; what on that face can be identified from outside; what changes character the moment it is identified. That stretch has to be walked face by face, and where it does not go through, coverage cannot be declared.

And this also answers what SAE's own line is held up by. Not by the ground. By one extra requirement on the downward path of cultivation: the direction of cultivation may not be identified from outside. Kant's path does not carry that requirement, so he is not bound by it. It does not follow directly from a person is an end. It has to be stated separately — and SAE had never stated it separately before.

6. Formal Legitimacy Fails Against the Strong

This is the one place in this volume where something must be criticized — and the criticism is not aimed at Kant. He wrote the problem down himself.

Appendix II of Perpetual Peace, the transcendental formula of public right: all actions relating to the right of other men are unjust if their maxim is not consistent with publicity. The argument is clean. A maxim that would defeat its own purpose the moment I announced it must be kept secret to succeed; I cannot publicly avow it without immediately provoking everyone's opposition. That universal resistance, foreseeable a priori, can only come from the injustice of the maxim toward all.

This is a real instrument. It asks nothing about motive and nothing about consequence. It asks one thing: does this maxim still stand once it has been said out loud.

And Kant writes down, immediately after, where it stops. The converse does not hold: we cannot infer that every maxim which survives publicity is legitimate — because whoever holds decisive superiority has no need to keep his maxims secret at all. One sentence, and the instrument's boundary is drawn.

The failure point is itself a structure, and that structure touches the ground. An overwhelmingly strong party can publish its maxim of oppression whole and without reservation. It survives the test: said out loud, it still stands — because its standing does not depend on the other side not knowing. It depends on the other side being unable. And so the formal test lets it through without a sound. While in that relation the other side has no position at all. It is informed, not answered; whether it accepts or refuses changes nothing.

7. What Is Criticized Is Making It Sufficient

The object of the criticism has to be fixed exactly, because this is the easiest place to fix it wrongly. The object is not Kant's instrument.

His negative formula of publicity is a sufficient negative condition — it serves only to identify when a maxim is unjust toward others, and he writes in his own hand that the converse fails. An instrument that can only say no, staying silent where it cannot say yes, is not thereby defective.

The object is the move that makes it sufficient. Mistake negative publicity for a sufficient or complete condition of legitimacy, and the oppression of the strong lands in its zone of non-determination — it survives the test, because the test was never in the business of issuing the verdict legitimate. The criterion did not fail. What failed is taking an instrument that can only say no for one that can say yes.

And the misuse is not hypothetical. An overwhelmingly strong party can publish its maxim of oppression whole and unreserved, and it still stands once said — because its standing rests not on the other's ignorance but on the other's powerlessness. In a system that recognizes only this one instrument, it passes. The cleaner the form, the more thoroughly it covers when it is mistaken for a sufficient condition. This has to be criticized, because it turns a person into something notified: formally complete, and in substance merely a means.

8. Publicity Is Not Encounter

SAE's answer: the criterion cannot fall on the form of the maxim alone. It has to fall on the character of the relation as well. Does the other side, in this relation, still hold a position from which a response could change something.

That sentence pulls publicity and encounter apart. Publicity is one party saying it out loud. Encounter is that, after it is said, the other's response can enter the matter. The strong party's publicity is the first and not the second. That publicity is a proclamation, not an encounter.

It also explains why SAE's yangmou — the open stratagem — is not the same as putting your cards on the table. Yangmou requires the other to take part as a clear-eyed subject, and taking part means his response has a position. Merely showing your hand while the other has no way to respond is not yangmou. It is proclamation in another form.

Kant gave the instrument, and marked where the instrument stops. SAE says: where it stops is exactly where the criterion should be.

9. Speak in Public, Be Taught in Secret

The second supplement of Perpetual Peace holds the book's only secret article: the opinions of philosophers on the conditions of the possibility of public peace shall be taken into consideration by states armed for war.

He then explains the arrangement inside it. The state will silently invite such counsel while keeping the fact of it secret — because to ask its subjects for rules of external conduct would seem to detract from the dignity of its legislative authority. On the philosophers' side, they must be free to discuss the general maxims of war and peace publicly; the sovereign should not let that class disappear or be silenced. Eight words: speak in public, be taught in secret. And he draws a line: it is not that the state must let the philosopher's principles take precedence over the jurist's — only that he should be heard.

SAE's Theorem Four requires that a warring party cannot but be questioned, and the questioning has to reach four layers: does questioning exist; does it reach the core of decision; is the questioner protected; does the questioning actually affect the decision.

Read Kant's article against those four. Questioning: yes. Reaching the core of decision: only adjacent — taken into consideration gives a duty to consider, not a position inside the procedure of decision. The questioner is locally protected: public speech may not be forbidden and the class may not be silenced, but there is no protection from reprisal and no procedural guarantee. Actual effect on the decision is not secured: no precedence does not mean no effect, and being heard does not mean being heeded. So it is a local mechanism, and it is not closed.

10. A Different Trade-off, Not a Right and a Wrong

The point is that Kant's misgiving is real, and he put it on paper: the state holds that admitting it needs instruction detracts from its dignity. He is facing a genuine trade-off — the mechanism, or the mechanism being acknowledged. He chose the first, and the price is that it cannot be seen. In his context, insisting on public acknowledgment might have meant no opening at all.

SAE chose the second, and its reason is structural too: an unacknowledged questioning cannot hold up layers three and four. Whether the questioner is protected, and whether the questioning really affects the decision, both depend on the thing itself being visible — an invisible questioning cannot be verified, and so cannot be found out when it is hollowed.

Two trade-offs, each with its price. Kant's price is that efficacy is unsecured. SAE's price is that in some contexts this requirement may keep the mechanism from being built at all. Nothing here is criticized, because the ground was not touched: Kant did not abolish questioning. He put it somewhere it could survive.

One thing is worth writing down all the same. Even the man who laid this ground, when he came to write the mechanism of questioning onto a state armed for war, hid it in a secret article. Not because he was insufficiently thorough. Because this requirement, the moment it lands on an actual structure of power, meets a specific resistance — dignity. Kant is the one who wrote that resistance out, which is why its shape is visible from him. Whether the resistance is universal across all traditions, the sample of this series is not yet complete, and no claim is made.

11. The Half Outside the Boundary

Three places: one divergence of path, one structure that had to be criticized, one trade-off made differently. They show the same thing. SAE and Kant share a ground, and the ground does not decide everything. Walking down from a person is an end, the choice of right or of cultivation parts into different lines at specific places, different landing points for the criterion, different trade-offs.

What this volume leaves SAE is not knowledge about Kant. It is a correction of SAE's own: a principle can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow automatically. The §18 firewall does not come straight down from the ground. It depends on one extra requirement along the path of cultivation — that the direction of cultivation may not be identified from outside — and that requirement had never been stated on its own.

The half outside the boundary in the title means this. Not that Kant wrote no criterion for conduct in war — he did. Not that right cannot handle subjects — legal personality, civic standing, future trust, he handled all of them. It is the layer that remains unsettled by those even after all of them are protected: whether a subject, inside the relation, still holds the position to question, refuse, revise, respond, and go on unfolding itself.

That layer lies outside the boundary of right. It is where cultivation takes over.

Materials, and Three Things Booked

Kant's Perpetual Peace is cited from the Mary Campbell Smith translation of 1903 — preliminary articles three, five and six; the first definitive article; the second supplement; appendix II. The Doctrine of Right is cited from the Akademie German — §57 (VI:347–348), §58 (VI:348–349), §59 (VI:349), §60 (VI:349–350). Chinese renderings are the author's own. Two version warnings stand: §60 opens with a parenthetical limiting the right against an unjust enemy in the kind of means while leaving quantity and degree unbounded, and a nineteenth-century English translation may have inverted quality and quantity there — wherever §60 is involved the Akademie German governs; and the Doctrine of Right has known scholarly disputes over editing and paragraph attribution, though §57–§60 were not found to fall inside them.

Two things are downgraded here rather than claimed. That §60 prescribes no procedure is registered as a textual fact only, with nothing inferred from it. And the step any external property condition displaces the subject of cultivation is not argued in this volume, so it is booked as outstanding: SAE may draw its line earlier than Kant, and it needs an independent argument to do so, and that argument does not yet exist. Until it is finished, the claim here is only that each line needs a further stretch of road — not that SAE's stretch has been walked.

One interpretive dispute is left unchosen — whether §60 is an independent exception in ius ad bellum or belongs mainly to ius in bello and ius post bellum — since neither reading affects the argument. And one debt is booked without an answer. Kant's exception for a divided state covers the case where a country splits in two, each part claiming to be an independent state representing the whole. When both parts claim in the first person to represent the whole, which bearing-position does do not perform the reconstitution protect? How is an outside actor to tell, without the telling itself completing the legislation for the whole? Kant gives when assistance stops counting as interference. What he does not give, and SAE has not given either, is how to identify the legitimate bearer among competing claims of representation.

This series keeps its own correction records in the body rather than repairing them silently, for a reason: a framework that requires cannot but be questioned must be the first thing questioned; and a text that shows no sign of ever having erred gives its reader no way to judge how its determinations were reached.

Abstract

This volume runs on two layers, and the point of it is that they cannot be run together.

Layer one: authorisation. Clausewitz and On Protracted War give constraints on war that share one form — war is authorised by an external political purpose and is therefore bound by it. SAE agrees with the content of both. But the form carries a premise neither states on its own: that the authoriser is itself stable, bounded, and does not expand. Neither authoriser satisfies it. So the form has a common limit — it cannot hold back the authoriser itself.

That limit is registered as a limit of the form, not as an internal failure. Neither party ever claimed its theory could bind the political purpose itself, so your constraint cannot hold back the authoriser is no internal criticism of either.

Layer two: the carrier. Machiavelli does not supply a third specimen of the same kind. He supplies a second-order stress test on layer one: even where the authoriser is itself constrained, the carrier that executes may form a war-interest of its own. Layer one asks whether the authoriser will move. Layer two asks whether, even with the authoriser still, the men who execute it will move on their own. Each layer has its own solution and its own insoluble part — and one layer's solution does not solve the other's problem.

1. War Is Sent Out, So It Must Report Back

Clausewitz and On Protracted War both hold that war should not swell on its own, and the constraint each gives takes the same form: war was sent out, so it has to go back and account to the thing that sent it.

Book Eight, chapter six B of On War puts the form most completely. War is nothing but a continuation of political intercourse with the admixture of other means; the phrase with other means is there to show at once that this political intercourse is not stopped by the war itself, does not change into something wholly different, but continues in its essence. And then: war has its own grammar, but not its own logic. Followed by the sentence that completes the form — war can never be separated from political intercourse; separate them in any way and the threads of the relations are to some extent broken, and what stands before us is a thing without object, meaningless.

Grammar of its own, logic from outside. That is the form.

On Protracted War is the one worth the closest look on this layer, because it writes the stopping condition down in plain words. War is the continuation of politics, put symmetrically: politics is bloodless war, war is bloody politics. And the stopping rule is indexed to the political purpose — the political obstacle removed and the political purpose attained, the war stops; the obstacle not fully removed and the purpose not fully attained, the war goes on. The stopping condition is not military opportunity exhausted and not the enemy destroyed. It is whether that political purpose has been completed.

So the two share one form: war is authorised by an external political purpose and is therefore bound by it. SAE agrees with both constraints. War really should not swell on its own. This is a real overlap, not a courtesy.

2. Machiavelli Is Not a Third Specimen

Machiavelli does not stand alongside the first two, and the reason has to be set out first. Clausewitz and On Protracted War give the authorisation and constraint of war by an external political purpose. Book One of The Art of War gives the incentive structure of the executing carrier. The two are not of one type — the first asks what authorises war, the second asks what the men who carry out war live on. Fold the second into the first, and two different levels get pressed into one.

His correct position here is the second-order stress test: even where the authoriser is itself constrained, the carrier that executes may form a war-interest of its own.

The material for registering it: in Book One, Machiavelli has Fabrizio Colonna argue that a well-ordered republic never allowed any of its citizens or subjects to practise war as a trade. The reason is not efficiency. It is a chain of incentives whose starting point is that the trade has no ordinary livelihood in peacetime, so those who depend on it must wish peace not to exist.

Two limits go with it. The speaker is Fabrizio, not Machiavelli in his own voice — the book is a dialogue. And what is forbidden is private livelihood, not knowledge of war: chapter fourteen of The Prince, in the author's own voice, says a prince should make the art of war his principal study. The two do not conflict.

3. Why the Two Layers Cannot Be Run Together

Layer one asks: will the authoriser move? Answer: yes. Layer two asks: even if the authoriser does not move, will the men who execute it move on their own? Answer: yes — as soon as their livelihood is tied to war.

The two have different solutions, and that is exactly what this volume needs from them. Layer one's problem has no solution here — the legitimacy of the authoriser is supplied from elsewhere. Layer two's problem does have one, and Machiavelli gives it: let no one practise war as a trade.

So this volume does not count him as a failed case. What he gives on layer two is a workable disposition. And the converse holds too: adopt his restriction, and layer one's problem is still there — the survival of a republic can equally demand conquest abroad.

Each layer has its own solution and its own insoluble part; and one layer's solution does not solve the other's problem. That sentence is all this volume takes from Machiavelli. The full treatment of layer two belongs to the question of how a means reworks the party using it, and that is not this volume's business.

4. The Other End of the Rope Is Moving

The form war is constrained by an external purpose carries a premise: that the authoriser is itself stable, bounded, and does not expand. If the authoriser can enlarge its goals in the course of things, then war must not exceed the purpose constrains only the distance between war and purpose — not how far the purpose itself has moved. The shape of the constraint is a rope, and the other end of the rope is moving.

Neither party states the premise on its own, because in each of their contexts it was too natural to state. And neither authoriser satisfies it.

Reason of state can be expansionist. Clausewitz's political purpose is the state's political purpose, and a state's political purpose can perfectly well be acquire more. War must not depart from the political purpose still holds — it merely constrains war not to exceed what the expansion requires. It cannot hold back the expansion.

A political purpose can upgrade itself. A political line redefines its goals in execution; that is not a betrayal of the line, it is the line's normal evolution. And after the redefinition, war is the continuation of politics still holds. What continues is the new politics.

5. The Clearer the Stopping Line, the Plainer What It Hangs On

And On Protracted War, precisely because it writes the stopping condition in plain words, shows the problem most clearly. Its rule is: political purpose attained, war stops. That is the only stopping condition on this layer that can be quoted, questioned, and checked afterwards — in that sense it is the best of the two.

And that plain stopping condition moves as the political purpose moves. Redefine the purpose and the stopping line shifts with it, while the rule political purpose attained, war stops needs not one word changed. So this is not a counter-example. It is the strongest positive example: the more clearly the stopping condition is written, the more plainly one sees what it hangs on. A plain sentence hung on something movable is still movable.

So the form has a common limit: it cannot hold back the authoriser itself. And the registration matters. This is uncovered / a limit of the form, not an internal failure. To call it a failure point would require first showing that the party had claimed some goal or criterion of its own — and neither ever claimed its theory could bind the political purpose itself. Clausewitz's theory sets out to explain what war is and how it stands to policy; On Protracted War answers how one particular war is to be fought. Your constraint cannot hold back the authoriser is an internal criticism of neither, because neither took that job. The object of the proposition is the form, not the men.

And this is not two men's separate oversight. Two different authorisers give the same limit, which says the limit does not lie in the choice of authoriser but in the form of taking authorisation. It takes both side by side to see it: read Clausewitz alone and you will think his reason of state was insufficiently pure; read On Protracted War alone and you will think it a problem with one particular line. Two systems with unrelated sources landing at the same place says the place is structurally determined.

6. One Objection, and How It Is Rightly Handled

The objection: Clausewitz was not naive. He knew policy could be bad policy; he says in the same chapter that if the policy itself is wrong, no correctness of military means makes up for it. So he foresaw that the authoriser is unconstrained, and simply held that this belongs to politics and not to the theory of war.

The objection holds, and this volume accepts it. To say ruling it out is exactly how the failure happens is a quibble: assigning a problem elsewhere is a legitimate declaration of range. This series makes heavy use of range declarations itself — silence on everything at the execution layer — so applying the same standard to a predecessor is the minimum.

So what this volume says narrows to one independently checkable sentence: after that declaration of range, what can the remaining constraint do, and what can it not. It can keep war from exceeding a given political purpose. It cannot make that political purpose itself constrained. Neither sentence is a criticism of Clausewitz. The first is his achievement; the second is what he expressly put outside. What is pointed out is only this: for someone who wants war constrained, this form alone is not enough — and that has nothing to do with whether his theory succeeds.

The correction makes the proposition steadier rather than weaker: it now needs no author's oversight, and denies no author's declaration of range.

7. The End of the Path

Ludendorff walks this path to its end: he swaps the authoriser from politics to the national will, and the criterion of the national will is itself. He expressly inverts Clausewitz's primacy of politics — politics obeys the commander, and the whole life of the nation obeys the war.

The consequences follow straight from the limit above. An authoriser that is its own criterion cannot say when to stop — the object of the war becomes the survival of the nation itself, which can terminate only in one side being destroyed in the sense of survival. It cannot tolerate any mechanism that tests it. And it cannot be falsified by any outcome.

The nature of the evidence has to be written down. The inference is drawn from the structure of the form, not from any particular formulation in Total War; the first-hand text was not obtained for this series, and the passages that would have turned on its specific wording did not pass verification and are not used. That material has been moved out of the release package as an isolated research item.

8. Cultivation Cannot Authorise Its Own Abolition

SAE's Theorem Two also constrains the widening of war: every widening has to pass the criterion again, and cannot carry on automatically because the last one passed.

Theorem Two does not take its authorisation from an external purpose. Its criterion comes from cultivation, and cultivation cannot authorise its own abolition.

A political purpose can demand that everything be sacrificed for it, including the very people it was meant to protect. A republic's survival can demand that citizens be turned into a supply of soldiers. A line can demand that individuals submit all the way down. Each of these demands is self-consistent in its own logic: an authoriser is entitled to dispose of what it authorises. Cultivation has no such entitlement, and the reason is categorial. Cultivation is not a goal. It is the very thing of a subject unfolding itself. A criterion that demands the abolition of that unfolding abolishes its own condition of holding. It is not that it violates cultivation. It cannot be said.

From which one operating discipline follows, for SAE itself: the criterion may not be hung on any particular good thing. The state's security, the republic's freedom, the people's liberation — hang it on one of those and you have an authoriser; and once you have an authoriser you have something it cannot hold back.

The discipline applies to SAE, and applies uncomfortably. It means SAE cannot say our criterion is there to protect the oppressed — that would make the interest of the oppressed the authoriser, and it can expand like any other. A criterion can only be a criterion.

9. A Criterion and a Reason to Mobilise Are Not One Thing

One thing is easily written down as a cost of that discipline, and it is not a cost. The discipline seems to make SAE's criterion hard to mobilise with: for the homeland, for liberation can be shouted, can send people to die; cultivation cannot authorise its own abolition cannot.

The difficulty's premise does not hold. The false premise is that a criterion and a reason to mobilise must be the same thing. Separate four layers and the difficulty dissolves.

A particular good can mobilise. What it cannot do is acquire, on its own, the standing to begin a war, to widen one, or to be exempt from review. What the discipline blocks was never people fight for their homes. It is those four words being taken to replace the threshold. A reason to mobilise enters the first layer and does not enter the second; it does not impersonate authorisation.

So the genuinely open question is a different one: how to let particular reasons for mobilising enter public action without impersonating the standing to authorise — a checkable division of labour between the language of mobilisation and the procedure of authorisation. That is a doable problem, not a dead end.

10. Where the People Stand in the Trinity

End of Book One, chapter one of On War: war is a wonderful trinity, composed of primordial violence, hatred and enmity — to be regarded as a blind natural force; of chance and probability; and of its subordinate instrumental character. The first belongs mainly to the people, the second to the commander and his army, the third to the government.

The arrangement leaves the people, in principle, without standing to question. The trouble is not that he put them in. It is where he put them. The people are the source of the war's energy, not its judge — and the consequence is structural: a corner constituted by blind impulse cannot be asked anything. You cannot demand reasons of a natural force. SAE's Theorem Four requires that a warring party cannot but be questioned, and that the questioning come from inside. Clausewitz's model has no such position.

This is not a belittling, and that has to be granted. Part of why he puts the people in that corner is that he had seen the mobilisation of the French Revolution — what he saw was a real, enormous force that had not existed before. His model describes that force accurately. What it does not describe is whether that force can ask a question.

11. Step Out of the Man, Into the Role

Book Three, on the military virtue of an army: to step out of this man and into the role that war assigns us to play — this is the form military virtue takes in the individual. And he adds that this virtue is a definite moral force, like any instrument whose effect can be calculated.

This sets the executor's no longer existing as a person, but as a role, up as a positive quality — and that touches a person is an end on one's own side.

It has to be put precisely. He is not praising coldness; he is describing how a good army actually works, and the description has an empirical basis — a unit that holds formation under fire really is acting by role rather than by individual reaction. The point of contact is the step of setting it up as a quality. Describing a phenomenon and setting it up as something to be pursued are two things, and he does the second: military virtue is a moral force an army ought to have, one that can be cultivated and can be calculated. The own-side half of the second formula is abolished there.

12. Friction: Two Faces of One Coin

Friction is usually taken to be Clausewitz's gift to SAE. It is — and it is at the same time something else, which has to be said first.

In war everything is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. These difficulties accumulate and produce a friction no one who has not seen war can accurately imagine. He gives the example of a traveller changing horses: at dusk you reckon on the last two stages, four or five leagues, nothing much; and at the second-to-last post there are no horses, or bad ones; then hills, bad roads, darkness — and after great trouble you reach the next stage to find wretched accommodation. Friction is the one concept that broadly corresponds to what distinguishes real war from war on paper.

But he says where friction comes from, very specifically, and that sentence changes everything. The military machine — the army and all belonging to it — is in fact simple, and appears on that account easy to manage. But we should bear in mind that no part of it is in one piece, that it is composed entirely of individuals, each of which keeps up its own friction in all directions. And then: a battalion is always composed of a number of men, the least important of whom, if chance so ordains, may occasion delay or even disorder.

Friction comes from this: an army is composed of individuals, and each individual has a direction of his own. And immediately after the description of friction, he writes the remedy. A powerful iron will overcomes this friction; it crushes the obstacles, but it also crushes the machine along with them.

The remedy he gives for friction and the definition he gives of military virtue point at one variable: how much of his own direction is left in the executor.

A stronger claim is not available, and has to be ruled out first. Someone will say: if friction comes from individuals each having their own direction, then reducing friction is reducing those directions — so an executor who has successfully stepped out of himself into the role no longer produces friction. That last sentence cannot be had, for two reasons.

First, friction is not one thing. The sources he lists fall into at least three classes — physical conditions; conditions of information and stamina; and individuals each having their own direction. Only the third bears on the executor's position as a subject. An executor wholly inside the role still meets bad roads, wrong intelligence and fatigue. He does not stop producing friction. He stops producing the third class. Second, no longer produces is a universal claim, and there is no material for it. Whether a man in the role never again hesitates, never adjusts by his own understanding, never pauses when orders and what he sees conflict — that is an empirical question about people, and neither this volume nor Clausewitz offers evidence.

So the only thing claimed is what can be read off the text: on the third class of friction, his remedy and his definition of virtue point the same way — reduce how much of himself is left in the executor. That is coherent in his own text, not stitched together here: friction is diagnosed in Book One, virtue prescribed in Book Three, and on the third class their directions coincide.

13. Three Classes of Friction

SAE accepts the concept, and it fills a gap of SAE's own. The four theorems are all at the layer of principle, and they assume by default that a criterion once set can be applied. §3 concedes the lightness of philosophy and the weight of the executor, but that is a concession of posture — it grants that the executor's task is harder without saying where the difficulty lies. Friction supplies that: at the front the criterion is not violated, it is worn away. Delayed information, distorted orders, fatigue, fear, weather, terrain — each degrades the input conditions for judging is widening now unavoidable. The criterion is still there. What is needed to judge it is not.

But SAE refuses his remedy, and not on moral grounds. Part of friction is not a defect to be eliminated, and that part is exactly the mark of the executor still existing as a subject. The narrowing has to be stated, because friction is very easily equated wholesale with subjecthood — and it is not one thing.

Only by folding the three into one does one arrive at friction at zero means the parts have been reduced to parts. That inference holds for the third class alone. So: the third class cannot be eliminated without abolishing the executor's position as a subject. The first two can be reduced, and reducing them abolishes no one.

And his own remedy still has to be criticized, because what he gives is a remedy that does not classify: a powerful iron will overcomes this friction — it does not distinguish whether what is to be crushed is bad weather or a subordinate raising an objection. And the half-sentence he himself wrote states the price of not classifying: it crushes the obstacles, but it also crushes the machine along with them. So what is criticized is not that he wanted friction reduced. It is that the remedy does not classify. He saw the price and took it for a price that must be paid. SAE says: for the third class, that is not a price. That is the abolition of the thing to be protected.

14. The Criterion Must Be Internalized Before the Friction

The third class cannot be eliminated without abolishing the executor's position as a subject, and all three classes wear away the conditions for applying the criterion. So that road cannot be walked by eliminating friction. What remains is: the criterion has to be internalized before the friction, not computed on the battlefield.

Deepening cultivation in peacetime is not only the accumulation of national strength. It is making the criterion into something that can be drawn on without on-site calculation.

What the inference does not claim has to be written down: it does not claim internalization guarantees correct judgement, and it does not claim internalized people will err in the same direction. What it claims is that some class of question can still be perceived, raised, and enter adjudication under pressure — and that is the only form in which a criterion still works outside its range.

A community that only starts wondering is this right once it is on the battlefield will have its criterion worn off, because that is precisely the moment when information is worst, time shortest, fear greatest. A community that has grown the criterion in during peacetime cannot have it worn off, because there is nothing there that needs computing. And this is taken from Clausewitz: he described the resistance; SAE turned it into a requirement on peacetime.

15. Left Unresolved in This Volume

SAE's criterion is hard to mobilise with is not an unresolved item — the difficulty's premise does not hold. What is genuinely open is a different question: how to let particular reasons for mobilising enter public action without impersonating the standing to authorise. This volume does not answer it, and it is a doable problem.

And one lesson on method goes with it: this series had previously taken this one cannot be filtered out as evidence that a boundary was working, when the actual reason it could not be filtered out was that the question itself had been put wrongly. A question that cannot be filtered out may be evidence that the boundary works — or evidence that the question was badly written.

Internalization handles only cases the criterion already covers. Meet a new situation it does not cover and friction's wear applies in full, with the judge in the worst conditions. That family of problems has been settled by division rather than centrally: the moment the criterion is most needed is the moment judging conditions are worst is ruled out entirely — it belongs to executive judgement, outside this series' range, and is acknowledged rather than booked as unresolved. The criterion must be internalizable stays inside — it is a question about how criteria are written, and internalization there has an exact meaning: move the criterion from the subtracting end to the adding end in advance, because on a battlefield there is no time to subtract.

And the trinity leaves the people without standing to question — while SAE has given no replacement model. In wartime, where does questioning come from, who protects it, how is it kept from being treated as sapping morale? This volume does not answer, and the question bears directly on whether Theorem Four can be operated at all.

Kant, Arendt, Machiavelli and SAE each give a mechanism for one and the same thing: a means reworks the party using it. The four act at different places and at different times, and none of them contains the others — each has cases the other three do not cover.

What this volume does not claim: that their coverages are disjoint, or that SAE's is the narrowest. What is proved is mutual non-containment, not mutual exclusion; and the four have heterogeneous domains, so there is no common ruler on which to rank them by width.

What is to be kept is one specific blind spot: §12 binds disqualification to information asymmetry, so an arrangement conducted in the open, with the executor fully informed, whose position as a subject is nonetheless abolished, gets no verdict from that criterion.

Three can be taken up, each differently. And the four together compose four angles of check for a list SAE cannot make on its own — but the four questions have to be preceded by a gate on the ground, because they screen what a means does to its user and cannot screen what an arrangement does to a particular person.

1. Four Mechanisms, Side by Side

Putting them side by side is the main move of this volume. Separately each looks like common sense; together it shows that they do not govern the same thing.

Kant: vices get carried into the state of peace. The sixth preliminary article forbids assassins, poisoners, breach of capitulation, incitement to treason. He gives six reasons, and the least-quoted is the sixth: these infernal arts, once employed, do not long remain within the limits of war. Take the use of spies — here one merely takes advantage of another's dishonesty; but such vices, once encouraged, cannot in the nature of things be rooted out, and will be carried over into the state of peace, where their presence will utterly destroy the purpose of that state. Note why he names spies. He writes it himself: here one merely takes advantage of another's dishonesty — he knows this is the most harmless-looking of the family, and picks it for exactly that reason. If even this one spills over, the heavier ones need no arguing.

Arendt: violence destroys power, it never creates power. She defines power as the capacity to act in concert — power belongs to a group and exists only while the group holds together. Violence is instrumental: it needs an external purpose to justify it, and its efficacy grows with the improvement of the instrument, independently of the number who hold it. Hence her judgement: violence can destroy power, but it can never create it; a regime that rules by violence has thereby shown that it has lost power. The time is immediate — not use it long enough and it spoils, but consumed in the very moment of use, because resorting to violence is itself the sign that the capacity to act in concert no longer suffices.

Machiavelli: those who live by war must wish war to happen. In Book One of The Art of War, Fabrizio Colonna argues that a well-ordered republic never allowed any citizen or subject to practise war as a trade — and what he gives is a chain, not a sentence. The trade has no ordinary livelihood in peacetime, so those who depend on it must wish peace not to exist. That incentive produces plunder: robbery, fraud, violence and killing are structurally attached to the trade. A commander's standing and income depend on war, so he has an incentive to deceive his employer to prolong it. When peace comes and such men are dismissed, they readily turn to armed adventuring and live by pillage. Whence a constitutional trilemma: a prince keeping professional soldiers in peacetime must go on fighting, maintain them indefinitely, or face a body of armed men whose livelihood has vanished. And loyalty attaches to the commander, not to the commonwealth.

SAE: the crux of gui is the suppression of one's own side's subjecthood. §12 says deceit is disqualifying not because it deceives the enemy but because maintaining an information asymmetry requires using one's own executors as instruments. If the executor knew the whole picture, the asymmetry could not be held; so to use deceit you must first keep your own people in the dark. One registration goes with it: the four-grade scale used here — mou, covert stratagem, open stratagem, deceit — had part of its legitimacy resting on a finding since withdrawn, that Sunzi had already made a similar distinction. The withdrawal is in volume six. Re-arguing the scale is not the interface series' business; it belongs to §12 itself, and this volume uses it before that argument is complete.
