2. Last Resort: a Moral Duty and a Structural Condition

The tradition's is a moral duty: you are obliged to try peaceful means first, and a ruler who goes to war without trying, even with just cause, is morally at fault. SAE's is a structural condition: cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue. That is not a duty but a judgement about a situation — whether those forms are still open.

A last resort of the duty type can be offset by exigency; one of the structural-condition type cannot. In moral reasoning the stringency of a duty is generally modulated by circumstance: I ought to have negotiated first, but they were already massing; there was no time is an available defence, and often an accepted one. Requirements adjusting to feasibility is not a flaw in moral reasoning — it is how it normally works. A structural condition admits no such adjustment. Urgency does not change whether those roads are still open. If the road of negotiation remains open and was not walked, Theorem One's condition is not met, however pressed the agent.

One practical consequence: at the moment when error is likeliest — the other side massing, reports confused, the window for decision narrowing — the binding force of a duty-type criterion is at its weakest, because that is exactly when circumstances did not permit is most persuasive. The criterion is loosest when it is most needed.

But one cost must be acknowledged. A condition wholly unmodulated by circumstance may in practice appear inhuman, and may require an agent to walk through a procedure that has become meaningless when he knows the other side is about to strike. SAE's only answer is that the condition asks not was the procedure completed but is that road still open — and a road the other party has closed does not count as open. But that answer pushes the burden of judgement back onto the agent — and the agent is in the position least fit to make it: angry, exhausted, afraid, and with good reason to think that waiting longer will kill him. These are not his faults; they are his situation. This volume does not solve that; it registers it. (The full treatment of that burden is in volume seven.)

3. Proportionality and the Bridge Clause: Intersection, Not Containment

Proportionality: the harm caused by a means may not exceed the value of the legitimate end pursued. The bridge clause: no means may foreclose the other party's possibility of reorganising itself as a subject of cultivation. The two block partly different things, and the bridge clause is not an upgrade of proportionality.

Direction one — the bridge clause blocks what proportionality does not. Proportionality is a judgement of magnitude, and it requires someone to put both sides on one scale. In war that weigher is usually the belligerent itself: it weighs the value of its own ends and the harm to the other, and every party will hold its ends to be of very high value. The bridge clause is a judgement of direction and needs no scale. It asks not how heavy was this blow but is that road still there afterwards. A belligerent may sincerely hold its end to be of infinite value; it cannot sincerely hold that a means which forecloses the other's possibility of reorganisation has not foreclosed it — that is a fact about the structure of consequences, not an assessment of value.

Direction two — proportionality blocks what the bridge clause does not. A military action that forecloses nothing yet is grossly disproportionate to its aim — heavy civilian casualties in taking a secondary objective, where those casualties do not destroy the other party's capacity to reorganise — draws no verdict from the bridge clause, and does draw one from proportionality. This must be stated plainly: SAE has a gap here. The bridge clause handles does it foreclose; it does not handle is it excessive. And excess is a real moral dimension, not something to be waved off with we do not make judgements of magnitude.

Direction three — the relation is intersection, not containment. So it is inaccurate to say the bridge clause is more fundamental or more thorough. They are two lines cut in different directions, and a system holding the bridge clause and not proportionality lets through an entire class of acts that ought to be blocked. Whether SAE needs an additional criterion of magnitude is not answered here — and the difficulty is that a criterion of magnitude requires a weigher, and admitting a weigher re-establishes the very position this volume declines.

4. Discrimination: the Premise of Rousseau's Version

Rousseau gives the most famous formulation, in The Social Contract I.4: war is not a relation between man and man, but between State and State, and individuals are enemies only accidentally — not as men, nor even as citizens, but as soldiers; not as members of their country, but as its defenders. And then the conclusion: since the object of war is to destroy the enemy State, it is legitimate to kill its defenders as long as they are carrying arms; but as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies or instruments of the enemy, and become once more merely men, whose life no one has any right to take. The reasoning is clean, and its force comes from that premise.

Rousseau's reason is the social contract: the parties to a war are two juridical persons, and individuals stand in an adversarial relation only while serving as units of war — lay down the arms and that status ends, and with it the adversarial relation. SAE's reason is different: the other party may not be struck out of the position of a subject of cultivation, whether or not he is at this moment serving as a unit of war.

Rousseau's principle of discrimination depends on the premise that both parties to a war are states, and fails in non-state war; SAE's does not depend on that premise. Rousseau states the premise very explicitly himself: in the same passage he holds that war between private persons can exist neither in the state of nature nor in the social state; that duels and private affrays do not constitute a state of war; that the private wars of the Middle Ages were an abuse of feudalism. He expressly excludes non-state violent conflict from war. So in civil war, insurrection, non-state armed resistance and decentralised resistance, individuals are enemies only accidentally does not obtain, because there are not two juridical persons.

The consequence is not hypothetical. The 15DD defence this series is concerned with is very often of exactly that kind: resistance in occupied territory, colonial revolt, self-defence in a society whose legitimate institutions have been destroyed. A slave uprising has no juridical personality — on Rousseau's framework the principle of discrimination does not apply there, not that it is violated, but that it does not apply. SAE's does not depend on juridical statehood, because a subject of cultivation need not be a state. And what Rousseau has that SAE lacks must be acknowledged: his reasoning yields an observable moment — the moment arms are laid down, a line both sides can identify. SAE's still exists as a subject of cultivation has no such moment; it requires judgement. In actual fighting, an observable line is more useful than a more correct line that requires judgement.

5. Legitimate Authority: a Reading Corrected

The tradition requires that only legitimate public authority may make war. An earlier version of this series read that as excluding the self-defence of the powerless. That reading is too broad, and it is corrected here.

Aquinas explicitly permits private self-defence. Summa Theologiae II-II q.64 a.7: an individual may use proportionate force to preserve his own life, even where the act foreseeably results in the assailant's death — provided the defender's intention is his own preservation rather than killing, and the force is not excessive. He says the act may have two effects: the preservation of one's own life, and the death of the assailant. The line he draws is elsewhere: a private person may generally not intend the assailant's death; intentional lethal coercion belongs to public authority acting for the common good. A soldier against an enemy, an officer against a felon, may intend lethal action under public authority — and even they are at fault if acting from private enmity.

So what auctoritas principis blocks is not the self-defence of the powerless. It is that a private act of defence does not automatically carry the juridical powers of public war — to initiate, to punish, to mobilise, to intend to kill. And Aquinas gives more than a slogan: a private person may not make war, because in a normal political condition he may assert his right before a superior's tribunal; nor can a private person summon the multitude that public war requires; conversely, the care of the common good is entrusted to public authority, which must repel enemies without as it uses public coercion against wrongdoers within. The substance of this gate is public jurisdiction, responsibility for the common good, and the prevention of a private quarrel being converted into public war.

6. SAE's Actual Distance from Him, and Where the Threshold Sits

The distance is smaller than it is usually taken to be, and that must be acknowledged. The four gates on the second face of Theorem One — do not open the second face on its own; see without substituting; genuine rising; the intervening party must have interests of its own — block the same class of things. An armed body claiming to represent the oppressed with no one having asked it fails the third gate; an intervener with no connection to the party intervened for fails the fourth; an action packaging a private quarrel as liberation fails the first. Aquinas's reasons are the same class of reason as what the four gates exist to prevent. To say that SAE rejects legitimate authority and is therefore more permissive is inaccurate.

The real difference is where the threshold is set: he sets it on the standing of the subject, SAE on the structure of the situation. Standing is a judgement about who this person is — does he hold public office, whence does his authority derive. Structure is a judgement about what this situation is like — has the carrier been lost, has the other party risen, is the intervener connected.

And the difference in range runs both ways. Direction one: a collective self-defence in a society whose legitimate institutions have been destroyed cannot be raised to the status of war under auctoritas principis — it may be an indefinite number of individual acts of justified defence, but it cannot be a war with standing to be initiated, to mobilise, to punish. And 15DD defence is very often exactly that situation. SAE's four gates do not ask this; they ask after structural conditions, and those have nothing to do with holding public office.

Direction two: standing is verifiable; structure is hard to verify. Does this king have the authority to declare war could be checked at the time; is the rising genuine requires judgement. This tells against SAE, and the cost must be stated: it is another appearance of one and the same problem — a structural condition is verifiable in principle while lacking, in practice, any settled way of being observed. The attribution of that problem divides in two: can this criterion be broken into publicly contestable sub-propositions is a question about the form of a criterion, and falls within what this series must answer; can it be broken down in wartime is an execution judgement, and does not.

7. Supreme Emergency: a Ground Conflict

Walzer holds that when the threat facing a political community is extreme enough to destroy its very existence, the limits of jus in bello may be breached. This is the strongest direct challenge to the bridge clause on means, because it does not claim the clause is wrong. It claims there exists a tier of exception at which rules give way to survival.

What supreme emergency permits is: to preserve our own carrier of cultivation, the other party's may be cancelled. SAE declines that permission and bears the cost of declining. The registration must be precise. To write this does not hold within SAE would not itself be wrong — it indeed cannot be uttered within SAE — but it reads as a determination that the concept is self-contradictory, and Walzer is not inside SAE, so that determination does not apply to him. The accurate statement is: this is SAE's choice of ground, not a determination about the internal consistency of the concept. Walzer's argument is coherent within his own framework, and he advanced it in full awareness of the difficulty.

The argument: the bridge clause prohibits foreclosing the other party's possibility of reorganising itself as a subject of cultivation — and what supreme emergency asks to exempt is precisely that class of means; it exempts what is ordinarily forbidden, which is to say the most thorough. So the content of the exception is: when one party's carrier of cultivation is threatened, the other's may be cancelled. And that cannot be uttered within SAE, for a reason of the same form as volume two's: cultivation cannot authorise its own cancellation. A criterion in the name of preserving cultivation whose content is cancelling the other party's cultivation cancels the condition of its own standing. It has not violated a rule; it does not obtain.

But the cost must be acknowledged, and the acknowledgement cannot be formal. Walzer's exception was not set down carelessly; it answers to a real situation — there are moments at which keeping the rules may mean the destruction of a community. SAE's refusal of the exception is the bearing of that cost: it issues no exception clause available to be invoked at such a moment, and a community in that situation gets no dispensation from SAE. That bearing must be written down; the situation may not be pretended away. And what SAE bears it on must also be written: not that the situation will not arise, but that once the exception is established, any party may claim to stand at that tier, and no one has standing to verify the claim.

8. That Position

The foregoing can be discussed item by item. One thing cannot, because it determines that the two are not of one kind. The full application of these criteria requires a position from which to determine who is the just party, and among states no such position exists. Just cause, right intention, proportionality — each of these judgements must be made, and among states there exists no maker of them whom all parties acknowledge.

The position then has only these destinations: left empty, and the criteria cannot be applied; occupied by the belligerents themselves, and each judges itself just, so the criteria lose their discriminating power; or occupied by some third party claiming standing — and whence that third party's standing? Historically the position has been occupied in turn by the Church, by the sovereign state itself after Westphalia, and in our time by something called international society. All three have had real functions, and all three have had their standing questioned.

9. Grotius Faced It Squarely, and SAE Stands on His Side

An earlier version of this series wrote that the position has only three destinations, and none of them holds. That exhaustive list omits a fourth, supplied here. Grotius knew clearly that among sovereign states there is no common judge of the kind available to litigants within a civil state — that absence is the very problem his theory of war addresses, not something he failed to see. And his answer has three tiers.

First, the tier of objective natural right: contradictory claims cannot both be true in the same respect, so objectively a war cannot ordinarily be just on both sides. Second, the tier of subjective culpability: a party whose cause is objectively defective may nonetheless act from excusable or invincible error — so objectively both sides cannot be just and both sides may have justified belief in their own justice do not conflict. Third, the tier of the law of nations: the law of nations may confer bilateral legal effects on a formal public war — the validity of capture, the standing of acts in war — even where the natural justice of the original cause cannot belong to both. The third tier does the most important work: it lets every soldier and every third party know which legal consequences of the war apply without first settling the dispute over just cause. So the fourth destination of that position is: do not adjudicate; govern conduct in the unadjudicated state.

The criticism that remains live is that the response yields no authoritative third-party determination. This tradition has no answer to the question does not. And here SAE and Grotius are on the same side, which changes the shape of this volume. Both decline to establish the adjudicating position, and both turn instead to governing conduct in the unadjudicated state. The difference lies in what is governed: Grotius governs the symmetrical distribution of legal effects — both sides fall under the same rules on capture, the status of prisoners, the validity of acts in war, without asking whose cause is objectively just. SAE governs whether the standing as a subject is preserved — the bridge clause asks whether, after the fighting, the other party can reorganise itself, and likewise does not ask whose cause is objectively just. Neither regime requires an adjudicator, and both are verifiable from outside. At this point SAE is not opposed to the tradition; it has taken another road in a direction the tradition had already opened.

10. Kant: the Position Cannot Be Established

Theorem One does not ask whether this war is just. It asks: has the carrier of cultivation been lost; can cultivation in its mild forms no longer continue; do the four gates pass. These are judgements about structure, requiring not standing but sight.

And Kant, from within Recht, holds that the position cannot be established. Perpetual Peace, Sixth Preliminary Article: war is only the sad recourse in the state of nature — where there is no tribunal which could judge with the force of law — by which each state asserts its right by violence; and in it neither party can be adjudged unjust, for that would presuppose a juridical decision; in place of that decision the issue of the conflict, as in a so-called judgment of God, decides on which side the right is. But between states no punitive war is conceivable, because there exists between them no relation of superior and inferior.

The position of this passage matters: it speaks from within Recht, not against Recht from outside. Kant does not say the moral concerns of just war theory are wrong. He says the adjudicating position does not exist among states — not ought not to be established but cannot be, because establishing it requires a juridical decision for which there is no judge, and because punishment presupposes a relation of superior and inferior which does not obtain. So SAE need not draw this distinction itself: someone on that road has already drawn it. (In the Doctrine of Right §60 of 1797 Kant employs the concept of an unjust enemy, which does not sit easily with this; that is treated in volume one.)

11. The Cost of Leaving It Empty

The cost of leaving the adjudicating position empty is that SAE issues no certificate of legitimacy usable to persuade a third party. Just war theory issues that certificate. It is one of the tradition's real functions and one reason it has been needed for two thousand years — a community deciding to resist needs to explain to its own members, to possible allies and to posterity why the thing is right. Our war is just is a sentence that can be said, quoted, and written into a declaration.

SAE's criterion produces no such sentence. What it produces is in this structure, entering war constitutes a cannot-not — a sentence meaningful only where the specific structure obtains, and acceptable only to someone willing to go and check that structure. This is not clumsiness of expression but structural necessity: once SAE issues that certificate, the adjudicating position has been re-established, because a certificate requires a signatory.

From this follows one requirement on the reader. The place where the four theorems are most easily conflated with just war theory is exactly where they most resemble it — high threshold, limits on means, peace as the aim. So it must be said flatly: the four theorems do not determine who is the just party. They tell no one you are right and he is wrong. They determine one thing: whether, in this specific structure, entering war constitutes a cannot-not, and which practices, once entered, turn the thing into something else. This determination faces inward — a criterion turned inward is reflection; turned outward it is judgement. A use of the four theorems to argue that one is oneself just, and the other unjust, has read them as a just war theory, and that is the misreading this volume exists to prevent.

12. One Asymmetry That Must Be Acknowledged

Leaving the adjudicating position empty does not exempt SAE from misuse. Anyone who wants a war can say the mild forms are exhausted, just as he can say our war is just. Both require external verification, and both are hard to verify in wartime. The difference is only this: the former can be broken into sub-propositions that can be publicly argued and separately evidenced — which roads were walked, what did the other party answer, which measures remain untried — while the latter points at a holistic judgement.

Three things must be stated precisely, because decomposability is very easily read as verifiability. First, each item after decomposition can still be disputed — whether a road was genuinely open, whether a given response constitutes closure, whether an attempt was sufficient: none of these has an automatic answer. Decomposability is not automatic transparency of fact. Second, what decomposability buys is localisation of dispute, assignable burdens of proof, locatable error, and a handle for revision — not the truth. Third, a holistic judgement cannot be refuted is also too strong: it can be opposed, there is simply nowhere for the opposition to take hold — an opponent can only deny it wholesale, and a wholesale denial is as unadjudicable as the wholesale assertion.

What survives the narrowing: SAE's criterion directs dispute toward places where it can be handled item by item, and just war theory's does not. This is an advantage of degree, not of kind. And the realisation of that advantage depends on someone actually asking — which is Theorem Four's business, and one of SAE's thinnest places.

13. Left Unresolved in This Volume

Proportionality blocks a class the bridge clause does not — foreclosing nothing, yet grossly disproportionate. Whether SAE needs an additional criterion of magnitude is undecided, and the difficulty is that a criterion of magnitude requires a weigher, while admitting a weigher re-establishes the position this volume declines. Without it, an entire class that ought to be blocked is not blocked.

Structural checks are harder to verify than checks of standing, and the attribution of that problem is handled separately. Supreme emergency is declined partly on the ground that any party may claim to stand at that tier and no one has standing to verify the claim — but the same words can be turned against SAE's own threshold, as this volume concedes. The difference is one of degree, and a difference of degree needs its size stated; this volume does not quantify it.

Finally: Rousseau's discrimination supplies an observable moment — arms laid down — while SAE's still exists as a subject of cultivation does not. Whether SAE needs an observable operational marker has not been considered.

Sunzi's counsel of caution and SAE's Theorem One overlap in conclusion, and the two criteria ask after different objects. Sunzi asks after the properties of the prospective war itself — what losses it will cause, whether they can be recovered, how much remains afterwards, how long it will take. Theorem One asks after the state of the relation before war begins — whether the non-war roads are still open.

From this: any factor that alters the properties of a prospective war may alter the output of Sunzi's criterion, and none alters the output of Theorem One — because such factors reopen no road that has been closed. This volume does not claim that technology makes war reversible, and makes no empirical claim about the effects of technology.

Nine Grounds' precept keep the officers and men in ignorance touches the ground of humanity is an end on one's own side and must be criticised. The verdict is absence rather than dismantling — within the materials examined, no prior self-limitation on one's own side is found available to be dismantled. And on the mechanism of that absence, this volume's original universal proposition is overturned by Mohism; the revised form is a hypothesis about institutional stability, and must be kept apart from the source of norms.

Theorem One's threshold condition — that attacking-the-plan and breaking-alliances be exhausted — depends for its determination on execution-layer knowledge, which SAE places outside its range. This dependency had not previously been registered. And one earlier determination is withdrawn: Sunzi never ranked mou above gui; that ordering was SAE's own taxonomy projected onto his text.

1. The Conclusions Overlap

Attack by Fire, closing passage — the place in the Sunzi that most resembles a self-limitation: no ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique. If it is to your advantage, make a forward move; if not, stay where you are. Anger may in time change to gladness; vexation may be succeeded by content. But a kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being; nor can the dead ever be brought back to life. Hence the enlightened ruler is heedful, and the good general full of caution. Calculations opens in the same direction: the art of war is of vital importance to the state, a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin.

SAE's Theorem One agrees with this conclusion. War may not be begun out of anger or humiliation — §13 makes this hard, excluding wars of honour and wars of revenge from the cannot-not. And the overlap is real, not a similarity of phrasing: both reject the same class of reason for war, those arising from a subjective state rather than from a situation. Both put it in the most conspicuous place — Sunzi at the close of the book, SAE in the first exclusion of Theorem One.

Where conclusions agree and criteria differ in kind, the two will diverge in identical circumstances — and finding those circumstances is what this volume does.

2. First, a More Convenient Contrast Must Be Excluded

The convenient contrast is that Sunzi's criterion is a mutually compensating weighing and SAE's a threshold. That contrast is unavailable, because it needs something Sunzi does not give. He supplies no weighting structure; a synthetic judgement need not be a compensable weighted sum; an irrecoverable loss need not figure merely as a weight.

So this volume adopts an axis that requires no such premise: what does each criterion ask after. The argument depends on no assumption about compensation, weights, or formulae — only on what three passages each ask after, which a critic can check passage by passage.

3. The Two Criteria Ask After Different Objects

Attack by Fire's reason for caution — anger may in time change to gladness, but a kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being — asks: what losses will this prospective war cause, and can those losses be recovered. Attack by Stratagem's taking a state whole is best asks the other face of the same class: how much remains usable afterwards. Waging War asks the same class again: how long this campaign will take, how much it will consume, whether it will bring in third parties. All three ask after one object: the properties of the prospective war itself.

Theorem One's two conditions are not of that class: has the carrier of cultivation been lost; can cultivation in its mild forms no longer continue. These two ask: before war begins, what state is that relation in — are the non-war roads still open. And the domain must be stated, because this is very easily read as a judgement about the whole Sunzi. It is not. The book contains a great deal asking after other things — form, force and vacuity ask after the balance of strength; Employment of Spies asks after channels of information; and the four rungs from the highest form of generalship is to baulk the enemy's plans downward ask after the available sequence of means, which stands closer to the state of a relation than to the properties of a war. This proposition claims only what each of the three passages asks after.

Not one of the three asks whether other roads are still open. And among Theorem One's two conditions, not one asks how great the cost of this war will be.

4. What Follows: Technology Can Loosen One and Cannot Loosen the Other

Any factor that alters the properties of a prospective war may alter the output of Sunzi's criterion; and such factors do not alter the output of Theorem One. The argument is analytic: Theorem One asks after the state of the non-war roads, and a technology that makes war cheaper, faster or more precise reopens no road that has been closed, and closes no road that remains open. It alters the side of the war, and Theorem One does not take its value from that side. So advances in military technology can, structurally, loosen Sunzi's class of criterion, and cannot loosen Theorem One.

What this does not claim must be stated. It does not claim that technology makes war reversible — death remains irreversible, and the losses to the attacked party's life, state and relations may remain irreversible; this volume makes no such claim and does not need it. It does not claim that precision and stand-off generally shorten wars — that is an empirical proposition, and this volume has no material for it. It does not claim that Sunzi's criterion will loosen to any specified degree — how much it moves is empirical; this volume states only that the direction of movement is fixed by what the criterion asks after.

And this is not a difference between strict and lax. Sunzi's can be extremely strict: give a kingdom destroyed can never come again into being enough weight and the requirement of caution can rise almost to a prohibition on war. Theorem One's can be extremely lax: read cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue broadly enough. The difference lies elsewhere — the two criteria change their verdicts when different things change. Sunzi's changes when the properties of the war change; Theorem One's when the state of the relation changes. And in practice these two kinds of change are not synchronised: technology can alter the properties of war enormously while the relation is untouched, and a relation can change utterly while technology stands still. So the two will diverge, and the moment of divergence can be stated in advance.

5. The Strongest Objection, and That Cancelling Operation

The objection: the li — advantage — in if it is to your advantage, make a forward move is not cost. Sunzi's li is a synthetic judgement. Waging War is not about casualties but about the structure of national exhaustion — a thousand pieces of gold a day; long campaigns leave the state's resources insufficient; blunted weapons and dulled ardour, strength exhausted and treasure spent, and then the other feudal lords will take advantage of your extremity to act. Third-party intervention and the international situation are matters at the level of relations — so assigning Sunzi's criterion wholly to the side of the properties of a war is too clean. The objection holds, and it is stronger than the version that merely says li is multi-item.

The response: the other lords will take advantage of your extremity is a judgement about what this war will bring on — what happens if it drags, what happens when strength is spent, whether third parties will move in. It asks after the consequence-structure of the prospective war. Theorem One asks what is already there in the relation before this war occurs. And the distinction can be drawn by one operation: cancel this war from the supposition, and Sunzi's questions have no object — if there is no campaign, there is no long campaign, no blunted weapons, no lords taking advantage. Cancel this war from the supposition, and Theorem One's two questions still have objects — whether those roads are open, whether the carrier of cultivation has been lost, hold equally in the case of not fighting, and it is precisely they that decide whether to fight.

One part of the objection must be granted: Sunzi's criterion does contain inputs at the level of relations. But they enter as components of this war's consequences, not as the prior state of a condition for going to war. The difference is not verbal — one and the same fact, that a certain lord is unfriendly, figures in Sunzi as he will take advantage if fighting starts, and in Theorem One as has the road of peaceful settlement thereby been closed.

6. The Tension Is Already Marked Within the Text

The closing passage of Attack by Fire in fact juxtaposes two different arguments. The irreversibility argument: anger may change to gladness, a kingdom destroyed can never come again into being. The advantage argument: if it is to your advantage, make a forward move; if not, stay where you are. The two are of different character. The former says a certain class of loss cannot be recovered and therefore may not be driven by what can be; the latter says move if it is advantageous. If the advantage is great enough, the latter permits war, while the former confers no veto — it requires caution, not prohibition. The effect of the juxtaposition is that the irreversibility argument no longer constitutes a veto on its own.

This step must be stated precisely, because it very easily slides back into the excluded model. To say that irrecoverability becomes a very weighty consideration is still the language of weighing. All this volume can say is a point about the text: the former sentence requires caution and does not require prohibition; the latter permits movement where there is advantage. Juxtaposed, the former does not acquire the standing of a veto — and that is read off the modality of the two sentences, without assuming any structure of weighing.

And the tension was not imported by an outside reader; it was felt within the transmission of the text. Giles notes here that if it is to your advantage, make a forward move duplicates Nine Grounds §17 and judges it an interpolation, on the ground that by sense anger may change to gladness should follow immediately on no ruler should put troops into the field to gratify his spleen. This volume need neither accept nor reject that textual judgement. What is worth noting is only that a commentator reading the passage line by line felt the two sentences to be discordant, and felt it strongly enough to propose a textual hypothesis.

7. Acknowledging the Cost: Questionability Is Not Computability

A difference is not a superiority, and one point tells against SAE. Theorem One's practical binding force depends on whether its two conditions can be questioned — and whether the carrier of cultivation has been lost, and whether cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue, have no settled way of being observed. They require judgement, and judgement can err and can be faked. A criterion that puts checkable items on the surface may in practice bind more tightly than one that is hard to verify.

This must be stated precisely, because it slides easily back into the calculation model. To say Sunzi's li can at least be computed by staff officers, and the resulting figures checked by others presupposes that his criterion has a computable form, and he gives no formula. What can be said is weaker: the items Sunzi's criterion asks after — how long, at what daily cost, in what state of morale, with what attitude among the other lords — several of them have relatively settled ways of being observed, so disputes about them are more readily localised. Whereas can cultivation in its mild forms no longer continue has no comparably settled way of being observed: who determines that a road is closed? What shows that it was open before? This is a difference in questionability, not in computability.

So the difference established here is a difference of object, not of stringency and not of reliability. Reliability is a separate question, turning on mechanisms of verification.

8. A Parallel Conclusion: Taking a State Whole

Attack by Stratagem: in the practical art of war, the best thing of all is to take the enemy's country whole and intact; to shatter and destroy it is not so good. So too it is better to capture an army entire than to destroy it… hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting. The sequence runs down to the smallest tactical unit, and the criterion throughout is one: whole is better than shattered.

Sunzi's reason is the usability that comes with wholeness. A country taken whole is still usable — its people, its produce, its walls, its fields are all there; shattered, there is less of it. Waging War has the direct counterpart: the enemy's spoils are used to augment one's own strength. A qualification must be entered, because this is easily read too narrowly: calling it a pure cost argument would be too strong — what quan preserves is not only convertible resources but structures of governance, populations, and the subsequent capacity to control the place. Nor is not-fighting a zero-cost limit: breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting requires investment in attacking-the-plan and breaking-alliances, requires the accumulation of positional advantage, requires the other side to accept. What this volume uses is the weaker step: Sunzi's preference for quan rests on there being a difference in usability between whole and shattered, and that difference can vary.

SAE's reason differs: war is itself an interruption of cultivation, so what is achieved without interruption is better in principle. This has nothing to do with how much remains usable afterwards. So: Sunzi's preference for quan rests on the state of affairs after this war is over; SAE's preference for not fighting rests on the interruption that war itself constitutes. The two ask after different objects, in parallel with the earlier finding — and any factor that alters how much remains afterwards may alter Sunzi's preference, while none alters SAE's: an interruption does not cease to be an interruption because much remains.

A possible objection: breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting exceeds cost calculation — it names a highest good, not an account. That reading has something to it, but the text will not support taking it so far, and the reason lies in the sequence. It does not appear in isolation; it is the apex of the preceding whole/shatter sequence, and every rung of that sequence asks the same thing: how much remains afterwards. If the apex asked something else, it would not be of a kind with the rest and the sequence would break. And the order Sunzi gives immediately after — baulk his plans, prevent the junction of his forces, attack his army, besiege cities — is justified in the same passage by how long a siege takes, what it costs, and that a third of the men are slain while the town still stands. What that reason asks after is still the properties of this war.

9. One Passage That Must Be Criticised

Nine Grounds: it is the business of a general to be quiet and thus ensure secrecy; upright and just, and thus maintain order. He must be able to mystify his officers and men by false reports and appearances, and thus keep them in total ignorance. And later in the same chapter: confront them with the deed itself; never let them know your design. The commentators are of one mind and are explicit. Cao Cao: the troops may share in the joy of the outcome, but not in the laying of the plans. Du Mu: the army knows only the orders to advance or retreat; it does not know the advantage to be gained by attack. Zhang Yu: war is the way of deception — and it is applied not only to the enemy, but there are also those who use the way of deception upon their own troops, making them follow without letting them know. Zhang Yu's note is decisive: deception directed at one's own side is not an interpretation brought in from outside but a position the commentarial tradition states of itself.

The practice advocated in Nine Grounds, in so far as it cancels the risk-bearer's standing to know his own situation and the character of his action, touches the ground of humanity is an end on one's own side, and must be criticised. The scope is limited, because this is easily written more broadly than the text supports. What the text plainly supports is the item cancelling the standing to know. What it does not plainly support, and this volume does not claim: that the practice also cancels the position of refusal — Nine Grounds does not discuss whether soldiers may refuse; that it also cancels the position of raising objection; that it covers every rank and every circumstance. Those may be offered as inferences, but must be marked as such and not written into the proposition.

Not falling within this proposition: withholding the timing and route of a march from outsiders; not making a specific point of attack public for a limited period; keeping particular sources of intelligence secret. These do not cancel an executor's knowledge of his own situation or of the character of his action. Falling within it: making an executor unable to know what kind of thing he is doing, or what situation he has been placed in. What Nine Grounds advocates is the latter — keep them in total ignorance, confront them with the deed; never let them know your design — which is not the keeping of one item of intelligence but the cancellation of the standing to know as such. And one inference, marked as an inference: a person who does not know what situation he is in, or what kind of thing he is doing, is in fact also poorly placed to raise a substantive objection or a reasoned refusal.

10. Three Things to Be Said Together

First, this precept is at the level of principle, not of technique. Keep them in total ignorance stands in Nine Grounds alongside quiet and thus secret, upright and just and thus orderly. It is not an incidental tactical suggestion but a specification of what kind of person a general is — calm, inscrutable, upright, orderly, and able to keep his own men in the dark. Four items in parallel, with no shift of register between them.

Second, it cannot be excised from his system. Same chapter: place your army in deadly peril and it will survive; plunge it into desperate straits and it will come off in safety. Placing an army where it cannot retreat, in order to make it fight to the death, is one of the central operations of Sunzi's doctrine of shi — and by the mechanism Sunzi himself gives, it is conditioned on the men not knowing the whole picture. No psychological universal may be added here: to say that an army which knows it is being deliberately placed in deadly ground will mutiny or scatter has no warrant — how an informed unit would react is an empirical question, and history is not short of cases of men who knew and went anyway. What this volume uses is a textual step: Sunzi himself wrote keeping them ignorant as the condition of this practice. Remove it and the mechanism he himself supplies no longer holds.

Third, the verdict is absence, not dismantling. By this series' discipline of determination, dismantling requires first showing that a self-limitation existed in that tradition to be dismantled.

11. The Evidence for Absence

Within the materials examined here — the Sunzi with its commentators, and the Sima Fa's Benevolence as the Root — no prior self-limitation on the side of one's own party is found available to be dismantled. The narrowing matters: to write the Chinese military tradition has no prior self-limitation on its own side would be a universal about a whole tradition, while this volume examined two books. The Wuzi, the Weiliaozi, the Six Secret Teachings, the Three Strategies and the later literature were not examined.

Evidence one: the self-limitations of the Sima Fa all fall on the enemy-facing side. Not to violate the seasons, not to march when the people are afflicted — this is to love one's own people; not to attack a state in mourning, not to exploit a natural disaster — this is to love the enemy's people; not to raise armies in winter or summer — this is to love the people of both. In antiquity, pursuit did not exceed a hundred paces, the following of a withdrawal did not exceed three stages; not to press the incapable, and to pity the wounded and sick; to form ranks and only then to drum. Six items, all of them regulating how the enemy is to be treated. Of these, not to violate the seasons, not to march when the people are afflicted does mention one's own side — but what it regulates is not raising armies in the farming season or during epidemics, a matter of not consuming one's own resources and strength, and it does not touch the soldier's standing to know or to judge.

Evidence two: the commentarial tradition reads the Sima Fa as a precedent for Sunzi's precept, not as its opposite. Cao Cao, commenting on Nine Grounds, cites the Sima Fa's on seeing the enemy, make the oath, and Zhang Yu reduces it to: your dispositions should not be divulged in advance. Within this commentarial tradition, the Sima Fa runs in the same direction as Sunzi on this point. Conclusion: within the materials examined, Sunzi is judged zero, not negative. He dismantled nothing; there was nothing on this axis to dismantle.

12. The Mechanism of the Absence, and That Rewriting

Having determined absence, one must ask why there is nothing on this axis. The original proposition: constraints on the enemy-facing side and constraints on one's own side have different mechanisms of generation. Enemy-facing, constraints can be generated by reciprocal equilibrium — that one does not strike a state in mourning, does not exploit disaster, can arise and persist because the other side observes it too and a violator will meet the same treatment next time. This requires no party to hold support at the level of principle: so long as the parties coexist over time, can identify violations, and are able to impose a cost next time, such constraints will arise of themselves and stabilise. On one's own side there is no counterparty to enforce — who redeems the soldier's standing to know, and who makes a commander pay after violating it? The soldier cannot punish the commander's deception, so deception is not reduced by being punished.

A compatible historical observation: constraints of this kind are more conspicuous in the Spring and Autumn period than in the Warring States — the lords of the earlier period coexisted over long periods, fought repeatedly, and knew one another, while the annexationist wars of the later period aimed at the elimination of the adversary, and the premise of repeated play weakened. The character of that paragraph must be stated: it is an explanatory hypothesis, not an established historical mechanism. The collapse of ritual restraint in the Warring States admits several explanations, and this volume has no material for excluding the others.

The original universal form of this proposition has been overturned. The counterexample: the Mohists were a transnational organisation whose internal discipline was enforced by no state's military law, and the Mozi's Lu's Questions records Mozi recalling his student Sheng Chuo from the service of Xiangzi Niu, who had thrice invaded Lu, on the ground that his salary outweighed his righteousness. This is a self-limitation on one's own side, and its support is not reciprocity. Mohism is a counterexample, not an addition. The revised form: self-limitations on the enemy-facing side can be stabilised by reciprocity; self-limitations on one's own side cannot depend on the other party's retaliation, and must be stabilised otherwise — by internal rights, procedures, membership structures, or institutional review. Reciprocity is not the only mechanism by which constraints are generated.

Two qualifications, so that the revision is not read too broadly. First, voluntary membership alone is far from sufficient — a whole bundle is required: rules acknowledged as constitutive of the community; an internal authority or review mechanism; real consequences for violation; exit a real and not merely nominal possibility; and a channel of appeal and reinterpretation. (Five candidate conditions generalised from a single sample, untested for necessity or sufficiency.) Second, why a norm holds and how a norm comes to be stably enforced within an organisation must not be run together. Humanity is an end does not require retaliation to hold, but it will not, by its normative standing alone, produce organisational discipline; conversely an office of Grand Master can stabilise discipline, which does not show that discipline to be grounded.

After the revision, one corollary is unaffected: a constraint hung on reciprocity is effective only on the face where reciprocity obtains; a criterion hung on humanity is an end takes effect without requiring the other party to be capable of retaliation. That is SAE's practical reason for placing its criterion on the ground rather than on custom — custom disappears where reciprocity disappears, and on one's own side there was never any reciprocity available. A constraint that takes effect only when the other party can retaliate is empty in every relation of gross inequality, and the internal relations of one's own party in war are the most unequal of all. And the five conditions all fail in a conscript army — membership is not voluntary, the cost of exit is death, there is no internal review, no channel of appeal, and the rules of military law are not acknowledged by the members but promulgated by the commander. So on the relation Sunzi treats, the conditions of generation remain absent.

13. A Dependency Registered

Theorem One's threshold condition — that attacking-the-plan and breaking-alliances be exhausted — depends for its determination on execution-layer knowledge. To determine whether that condition is met, one must know what options those two comprise; and their concrete practice — how to disrupt the other side's designs, how to break up his alliances, what methods are available, under what conditions each is feasible — falls precisely within what this volume's scope note places outside SAE's range.

This does not refute Theorem One, but it stands in tension with §4's the layers do not compete. The threshold condition itself is given by principle — have the other roads been walked is a question of principle; whether it is met must be certified by execution-layer knowledge. A layer of principle may declare that it does not do the execution layer. It may not declare that it does not depend on one.

The practical consequence is not abstract. An agent who does not know what methods attacking-the-plan and breaking-alliances comprise cannot judge whether he has exhausted them. He will conclude there is no road while roads remain — and preventing exactly that is what Theorem One is for. A sincere agent of limited judgement may, in perfect good faith, cross a threshold he should not have crossed, simply because he did not know there was another way. Theorem One cannot prevent this by itself. This dependency had not previously been registered; whether to feed it back into the treatise, this volume does not answer.

14. One Correction, and a Load-Bearing Member

In earlier work this series read Sunzi as ranking mou above gui, and on that basis held that he possessed, in the hierarchy of means, a self-limitation oriented toward 15DD. That reading does not hold and is withdrawn here. The grounds: first, Attack by Stratagem's sequence ranks objects of attack — his plans, his alliances, his army, his cities — and the reason for the ranking is the properties of the war. Second, Calculations' all warfare is based on deception states a mode of operation, and the position in which it appears is decisive: the first chapter, as a general proposition, followed immediately by concrete practices — feign incapacity when able, appear far when near. Third, a general proposition applies to every rung of the sequence, attacking-the-plan included; indeed the commonest way of disrupting an opponent's plan is to make him believe something false. So mou and gui are two orthogonal axes and do not form a ranked sequence. That sequence is SAE's own four-rung taxonomy projected onto his text.

The methodological consequence must be recorded alongside. To project one's own taxonomy onto another's text, and then discover there a tendency oriented toward one's own position, is a self-confirming operation — it guarantees that the observer will always find himself in others. The credibility of such findings is zero, because they cannot fail. The error persisted through several rounds and was found only on returning to the text; and what found it was not finer reasoning but setting out the original position and context of two sentences.

And a downstream consequence: part of a load-bearing member's support has moved. With Sunzi ranked mou above gui withdrawn, the question arises whether SAE's four-rung hierarchy of means has support independent of Sunzi — its legitimacy previously depended in part on the attribution that Sunzi had already drawn a comparable distinction, and that attribution is now withdrawn. Two volumes of this series rest on it: volume three, whose recoil mechanism and first test question issue from §12; and volume seven, whose matching of Gandhi's satyagraha rests on one rung of the hierarchy. Each carries a registration; and the re-argument of the hierarchy itself belongs to §12 of the treatise, not to this series. This series can point out the gap; it cannot fill it.

15. Left Unresolved in This Volume

Whether the registered dependency should be fed back into the treatise is undecided. If it is, the tension with the layers do not compete must be handled; if it is not, an account is owed of how a user of Theorem One is to determine exhausted without commanding execution-layer knowledge — and no such account exists. Related to this is the question of verifiability: Theorem One's binding force depends on whether its two conditions can be questioned, and neither has a settled way of being observed. The two are two faces of one thing — Theorem One needs something it does not itself supply.

The revised form of the proposition about generation has the support of only one strand of the Chinese tradition. Until at least two more strands have been run, it is used as a proposition awaiting verification — German military thought, Islamic siyar jurisprudence and Indian political thought have not been examined.

Finally, an inference this volume cannot verify: the high frequency of borrowed-ground self-limitations on one's own side — those supported by religious command, ritual, or codes of honour — may have a structural explanation: that face has no reciprocity available, and can only borrow a ground from elsewhere. Unverified.

Abstract

Gandhi and SAE are structurally joined at one point: both refuse to reduce the other party to a disposable thing, and neither retreats in the face of domination. But that does not make the ground the same — Gandhi's path carries other weight of its own: truth, non-violence, self-suffering, and conversion rather than coercion as the aim.

The position of disagreement is not whether to act, but that the two criteria have different principal trigger variables. Gandhi's path is triggered by the character of the action itself and the standing of its practitioners — is the cause just, can these people hold the discipline, has violence broken out, is the aim conversion or coercion. SAE's Theorem One is triggered by the channels of relation and the other party's conduct — are the mild forms still open, what did the other party give in answer, has the carrier of cultivation been lost.

Two stronger claims do not hold. That Gandhi's boundaries are determinable without knowing who the adversary is — they are not; all four require facts and a situation. And that he does not respond to situation and carries no burden of judgement — that is writing a different path as a correction of it. The difference is not that one requires judgement and the other does not, but that the objects of judgement differ.

And SAE must acknowledge two costs: the judgement have the mild forms been exhausted falls on the person least fit to make it; and SAE chose a path that issues a permission, and must therefore bear that permission's misuse — though what Gandhi's path is immune to is one specific misuse, not misuse as such.

1. He Is Not Naïve, and This Must Be Established First

The commonest misreading of Gandhi treats non-violence as a soft or morally fastidious choice — one does not act because one cannot bear to. It is not that. Satyagraha means, literally, holding to truth, and its actual content is a structured method of confrontation. Conducted openly: actions are announced in advance, intentions are not concealed, no surprise is manufactured. Without deception: no false appearances are created. Bearing rather than inflicting: the consequences of defiance are borne — arrest, beating, dispossession — rather than transferred to the other party. And leaving the other a way out: the aim is not to make him submit or be shamed. His own formulation — a satyagrahi's object is to convert, not to coerce, the wrong-doer.

This is not the avoidance of conflict but another way of entering it, and a very costly one. It forbids exactly what pressure most naturally produces. One item is not on that list, and its absence must be stated: does not exploit the other party's mistaken information has not been confirmed as a canonical rule of Gandhi's. The confirmed neighbouring principle is refusing to embarrass an opponent and refusing to take advantage of his difficulties — which concerns not taking unfair advantage, not the non-exploitation of an informational asset.

And this volume makes no ranking of strictness. To write that satyagraha's discipline is stricter than that of violent resistance is an unavailable comparison — the two disciplines require different things (one requires not striking back and continuing to bear; the other requires obedience and coordination), and there is no common scale on which to rank them. This volume does not need such a judgement.

2. What the Same Side Precisely Means

Gandhi and SAE are structurally joined at the point of not reducing the other party to a mere instrument; but it does not follow that the disagreement between them has nothing to do with grounds. To write the disagreement cannot be explained by a difference of ground would read a structural join as an identity of ground. Gandhi's path carries other weight: truth, non-violence, self-suffering, and conversion rather than coercion as the aim. These four are not SAE's ground, nor derivable from it.

In the earlier volumes of this series the divergences occur where the grounds differ — an external purpose as authoriser is not of a kind with cultivation; a criterion landing in Recht is not of a kind with one landing in cultivation; whether to establish a position from which to determine who is the just party; an honour system is not of a kind with cultivation. This volume is not like that. He treats a person as an end: conversion rather than coercion is precisely the refusal to reduce the other to something disposable. He does not retreat before domination: the whole content of satyagraha is not retreating, only not retreating by way of striking back. And he requires that his own executors be lucid, willing, and aware of what they are doing — on this he is more explicit than SAE. So this volume's disagreement must be found elsewhere, and finding it is its main work.

3. Openness and Non-Deception: Close Correspondence, Different Reasons

§12 of the treatise divides means into four rungs — stratagem, covert stratagem, open stratagem, deception — and the requirements of open stratagem correspond almost item by item to the first three of satyagraha's: openness, no reliance on an information gap, the other party participating as a lucid subject. The two correspond closely in operational demands, and their reasons differ.

Gandhi's reason is truth: means and end are not separable, and a result reached by deception has deception already in it; and truth can only be held to, not imposed, so confrontation must take place where both parties can see. SAE's reason is cultivation: the defect of deception is that it must use one's own executors as instruments — maintaining an information gap requires one's own people to be uninformed — and conducting things openly means the other party remains in a position from which to respond, which is what the other party still exists as a subject of cultivation concretely amounts to.

One registration is required here. The four-rung hierarchy used in this section previously drew part of its warrant from a withdrawn attribution — that Sunzi had already ranked stratagem above deception on the same axis. Volume six has withdrawn it: Attack by Stratagem ranks objects of attack, while all warfare is based on deception states a mode of operation and is set down as a general proposition about all warfare; the two axes are orthogonal and form no ranked sequence. The re-argument of the hierarchy itself does not belong to this series; it is a matter for §12 of the treatise. This volume uses it while that argument remains incomplete.

4. One Comparison Withdrawn

One apparently available proposition is not asserted here: that Gandhi's criterion is stricter than SAE's, forbidding all deception, including such things as concealing a line of march. It does not stand, and the reason is this volume's own: does not exploit the other party's mistaken information has not been confirmed as a canonical rule of Gandhi's, and that proposition would be built on it. To use as a load-bearing member something one has oneself marked unverified is a missing premise.

What remains: satyagraha does require that action be announced in advance and that no false appearance be created. But how far those requirements extend — whether they reach as far as military secrecy about a line of march — this volume has no material to determine, and Gandhi was not in a position that required him to say. So the comparison of the two criteria's breadth is not made here, and the disagreement below does not depend on it.

5. Bearing Is Not Self-Destruction

§19 of the treatise forbids completing a gesture by way of destroying the carrier of cultivation. On the surface this conflicts with bearing; in fact it does not. Gandhi's bearing is not self-destruction. It keeps the cost on one's own side rather than transferring it to the other, while preserving that community's capacity to go on acting — those arrested come out; the movement continues.

This series has given the distinction elsewhere: the line between preserving the carrier and mere acquiescence lies not in the magnitude of the cost but in whether, after the concession, the standing as a subject has been handed over. By that line, Gandhi's bearing falls on the side of preserving the carrier: what those who bear surrender is bodily liberty, not the position from which they decide their own direction. The movement continues, and its direction is still set by the participants. And this point SAE should acknowledge more plainly: refusing self-destruction is not refusing to bear costs. The distinction is whether, after this act of bearing, that subject is still there.

6. Gandhi Does Have Boundaries, and Strict Ones

One formulation must be excluded first: to say that on Gandhi's path exhaustion does not arise in principle, and to take him to set no boundaries, is inaccurate. At least four boundaries are confirmed. First, the cause must be just — there can be no Satyagraha in an unjust cause (Young India, 27 April 1921). This is not advice but a condition of qualification.

Second, the practitioners must be fit: even where the cause is just, if the participants lack the capacity to suffer continuously, to hold discipline, and not to strike back, the method cannot be carried. Third, an outbreak of violence is a reason to suspend, not to escalate. Where a mass action is accompanied by violence, his response is suspension, not treating violence as the next stage of the same method — this is particularly important: it shows he did not fail to consider escalation but expressly refused it. Fourth, the aim is conversion, not coercion: an action aiming to make the other submit is not satyagraha, however non-violent in form.

So he is not absolutely non-violent without regard to conditions. He has a fairly strict set of conditions; they simply are not all in the same place.

7. What the Boundaries Are Triggered By

Within the materials examined by this series, no boundary of Gandhi's was found that is triggered by the character or obduracy of the adversary. The reason for the narrowing must be given: to write no boundary triggered by the adversary is to be found makes it a negative proposition whose warrant is that a search did not find one — while this series has elsewhere accepted the contrary discipline, that a negative proposition may not be raised from not found to does not exist. The same standard must apply to itself. So this is limited to: not found within the materials examined, and used as a proposition awaiting verification.

SAE's boundary is at the other end. Theorem One's threshold: the carrier of cultivation has been lost; cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue. Mild forms includes satyagraha, and it is among the most powerful of them. Theorem One requires that they be exhausted — a subject that has not seriously attempted open resistance and non-violent non-cooperation does not meet the condition for war. And have they been exhausted must be judged in a particular situation: are these roads still open in this situation, what did the other party give in answer to each approach, what measures remain untried.

So the position of disagreement is not whether to act, but that the two criteria have different principal trigger variables.

8. The Difference in Trigger Variables, and Two Traps

Gandhi's path is principally triggered by the character of the action itself and the standing of its practitioners — is this cause just, can these people hold the discipline, has violence broken out, is the aim conversion or coercion. SAE's Theorem One is principally triggered by the channels of relation and the other party's conduct — are those mild forms still open, what did the other party give in answer to each approach, has the carrier of cultivation been lost.

Trap one: using subtracting conditions and adding conditions as an exhaustive classification — that is, writing that Gandhi's four boundaries can be determined without knowing who the adversary is. That does not hold. Whether a cause is just requires knowing what the cause is directed at, what it demands, whom it will affect; whether practitioners are fit requires knowing what these particular people have been trained in and what they have borne; whether violence has broken out is a pure question of fact. All of these require facts and a situation — and this series' own working note says it: subtracting and adding conditions are dominant directions, not an exhaustive classification of every act.

Trap two: taking Gandhi does not respond to situation and carries no burden of judgement for a property of his path. This is writing a different path as a correction of it. Gandhi likewise faces difficult judgements: whether a cause is just is a judgement of qualification; whether participants can hold is an organisational judgement; whether violence has broken out far enough to require suspension is a judgement of fact. He too must make these under pressure, and can get them wrong. So the difference between the two paths is not that one requires judgement and the other does not; it is that the objects of judgement differ.

Two conclusions still stand, with their reasons restated. First, why on Gandhi's path the question of exhaustion does not arise in the same form: not because his judgements need no situation, but because his trigger variables do not point at the adversary — however obdurate the other party, that does not change the answer to is this cause just. Second, why SAE must deal with the trouble of verifiability: because its trigger variables point at the other party's conduct and the state of the relation, and facts of that kind are the hardest to verify in wartime, the easiest to misread, and the easiest to misread with motive. This is not an oversight; it is the necessary cost of putting the trigger variables there.

What it principally asks

9. The Difference Itself Constitutes No Superiority

This must be stated, because this section is the easiest to read as SAE is more realistic. Placing the trigger variables on one's own action and the fitness of practitioners has the advantage of stability — it does not move with the other party's conduct; however brutal the adversary, that cannot make an unjust cause just, nor an undisciplined body fit. The cost is insensitivity to changes in the state of the relation.

Placing them on the channels of relation and the other party's conduct has the advantage of responsiveness — it can distinguish an adversary still negotiating from one already killing. The cost is that it can be distorted by those changes, and that the moment it is most needed is the moment it is hardest to determine correctly. Each has its own mode of failure, and the two modes cannot judge one another.

10. The First Cost: the Burden Falls on the Least Suitable Person

SAE hands the judgement have the mild forms been exhausted to the party concerned, and that party is in the position least fit to make it. He is angry, exhausted, afraid, and has good reason to think that waiting longer will kill him. These are not his faults; they are his situation.

One thing must be stated precisely: to say Gandhi's path does not have this problem, because it does not require this judgement, does not hold — he too must judge, under the worst conditions, whether the cause is just, whether the body can hold, whether violence has broken out. What does hold is a weaker sentence: the judgements on his path do not point at the adversary, and so are not beset by that class of question which is hardest to verify and easiest to misread with motive — is the other party deceiving me, does this exchange count as a closure. That is a real difference, but it is not he carries no burden of judgement.

SAE has only two things to meet this with: Theorem One's four gates, and Theorem Four's questioning. Both are of limited force — the gates must be passed by someone, the questioning must be done by someone, and wartime is when fewest are willing to ask. And part of this burden does not fall within what this series should answer: whether there is time to ask is an execution judgement. But whether this criterion can be broken into publicly contestable sub-propositions is a question about the form of a criterion, and that part stays inside — and that this series does not make execution decisions does not thereby cost it the standing to question them.

And on this Theorem One is decomposable: which mild forms existed? when was each closed? who closed them? what traces were left? what did the other party give in answer to each approach? So the accurate shape of the cost is: the whole of the judgement falls on the party concerned, while the decomposition of it can be questioned from outside. SAE can offer no help with the former; with the latter it can.

11. The Second Cost: SAE Chose a Path That Issues a Permission

SAE's criterion outputs a may, and it must therefore bear that may being misused and abused. The mild forms have been exhausted can be said by anyone who wants a war. And the difference of Gandhi's path on this point must be stated exactly. To say Gandhi's path will not be abused in this way is too strong — any set of claims can be abused; a non-violent movement can equally be used to suppress internal dissent, to require of others a cost they should not have to bear, or to justify inaction.

What does hold is narrower: his set of claims cannot be used as a licence for escalation to violence. However just the cause, however brutal the adversary, what it outputs is never we may now fight. That is a real difference, and not to be waved away with more realistic; but it is immunity to one specific misuse, not immunity to misuse as such.

SAE can say only one thing here, and it is a difference of degree, not of kind: the mild forms have been exhausted can be broken into publicly contestable sub-propositions; our war is just cannot. And the content of that sentence requires no subsequent retraction: each item after decomposition can still be disputed; decomposability buys localisation of dispute, assignable burdens of proof, locatable error, and a handle for revision — not automatic transparency of fact; and the latter is not irrefutable but has nowhere for opposition to take hold. And the realisation of that advantage depends on someone actually asking — which is Theorem Four's business, and one of SAE's thinnest places.

12. What He Has and We Lack

A whole body of operational discipline, and the experience of executing it. §12 of the treatise defines open stratagem clearly but says nothing about how it is done. Gandhi did it for decades, and what he left is concrete: how actions are announced in advance; how discipline is maintained among tens of thousands of participants; how participants are trained not to strike back even when struck; how a movement continues after its leaders are arrested; and — hardest of all — how a movement is suspended once violence accompanies it, rather than allowed to slide into escalation.

In the open-stratagem rung of the four-rung hierarchy, SAE has a definition and no instance. No one has filled that rung more fully than Gandhi. And this does not belong to the execution layer, outside our range: it is not knowledge of force levels and terrain but knowledge of how a community keeps itself open, non-deceiving, and refraining from expelling the other party from the position of a subject, under extreme pressure — which is exactly the question of how something at the level of principle comes to be enacted, and falls in the middle of the axis, the stretch both ends must walk.

One limit of verification must be noted: it could not be confirmed that a written code of discipline exists in Gandhi's own hand containing simultaneously no deception, actions announced in advance, and do not exploit the other party's mistakes. Most circulating Gandhian rules are compilations made by others from statements of different periods. The operational discipline described here is therefore of uncertain written form, though its actual execution is amply recorded.

13. Where Each Path Halts

Both paths halt at the boundary of their own criteria, and what each leaves beyond that boundary differs, as does whom it is handed to. SAE states the conditions of the cannot-not, not whether they are met at this moment. The latter is not judged by a single subject, and must be handled by a threefold distinction: an execution decision is made by actors with the actual information and institutional responsibility; those bearing the risk retain a position from which to speak and refuse; outside critics retain standing to question. And what the person making that execution decision must handle — the clock, the fear, the incomplete intelligence, the question there was no time to ask — this series cannot supply. But this series cannot supply the execution judgement is not this series may not question it. Standing to question does not lapse for want of having borne the same consequences.

And Gandhi's path likewise halts: what he gives are conditions of qualification for a method — is the cause just, are the practitioners fit. He too cannot judge, for a particular community, whether it can still hold that discipline at this moment, or whether the moment for suspension has come.

One closing sentence is unavailable: both paths hand it here to the same people, and for the same reason — those who do not bear the consequences do not make that judgement. Two things in it do not hold. First, the reason itself does not hold: it merges three kinds of standing — the authority to decide, the position of those bearing the risk to speak and refuse, and the standing to question and criticise — into one, and once merged it collides head-on with the rule that execution may not cancel a criterion by appeal to being on the spot. Second, what each leaves behind and whom it is handed to both differ. So the comparison is not handed to the same people at the same place. It is: both walked to the boundary of their own criteria, and what lies beyond differs — and put this way the comparison is more useful, because it shows what each path leaves to practice, whereas handed to the same people shows only that both stopped.
