GandhiA set of conditions of qualification for cause and practitioners, plus a disciplineThose maintaining the discipline, and those organising the movement

14. The Sentence This Volume Keeps

When SAE says cannot-not, it is not saying you are naïve. It is saying: I do not assume the oppressor will see.

And that sentence needs a qualification at once, because a false dichotomy is very easily made here: namely, that if bearing can indeed move any oppressor, if there exists no machinery of domination able to run without an audience, then this whole road of SAE's must be walked again, and Gandhi's path is right. That dichotomy misstates both sides.

It misstates Gandhi: the working of non-violence does not rest only on moving the oppressor. It can work by raising the cost of ruling, by altering third parties and international opinion, by dissolving the cooperation of those who carry out orders, and by maintaining a community's organisational capacity through the bearing. Whether the oppressor can be moved is not the sole condition of that path's holding. It misstates SAE: SAE's cannot-not does not rest only on the empirical judgement that oppressors will not be moved. Theorem One's threshold also contains the condition of whether the carrier of cultivation has been lost, and that has nothing to do with whether the oppressor can be touched.

What holds after the narrowing: SAE does not assume that every structure of domination necessarily contains a position that can be touched — and that remains a judgement about the world, and may still be wrong. If it is wrong, part of Theorem One's threshold requires re-argument; but that is not the same as the whole road having to be walked again, nor does it make the other path automatically true.

15. Left Unresolved in This Volume

The distinction between the whole of the judgement and the decomposition of the judgement holds that SAE can offer no help with the former. But decomposition too must be carried out under pressure — can a community under siege break have the mild forms been exhausted into five specific questions at that moment? Not answered.

This may not be registered as Gandhi's criterion is the stricter; whether SAE should tighten is not considered — that premise was excluded above, since it would rest on a rule this volume itself marks unverified, and a proposition that does not stand cannot serve as the premise of an unresolved item. What remains open is narrower: should SAE's criterion for open stratagem extend to forbidding all deception? But that question can no longer be raised by way of Gandhi — this volume has no material to determine how far satyagraha's requirements extend into military secrecy. It must be raised on SAE's own reasons, and this volume has not found them.

Two further items: the proposition about trigger variables is a negative proposition awaiting verification — not found within the materials examined, not shown not to exist. And the operational discipline described above is of uncertain written form: if some item proves to be a later compilation rather than Gandhi's own position, the discussion involving it must be revised.

Abstract

Nitobe Inazō's Bushido: The Soul of Japan (1899) agrees with SAE on the question of living and dying to a degree beyond what is usually expected: he writes plainly that to hasten death or to court it is alike cowardice; that to die for a cause unworthy of dying for is a dog's death; and he quotes, approvingly, that where life is more terrible than death it is the truest valour to dare to live.

SAE's prohibition on self-destruction overlaps with him in conclusion, with a different reason. His is the proper use of honour; SAE's is that a subject's own termination also terminates the relations and undertakings that unfold on condition of him, for which he bears responsibility. And the difference in range can be named: his criterion ceases to block where honour genuinely requires death; SAE's still blocks.

The divergence is concentrated at one place, and it is one he argued for himself: in the Sugawara story a child is delivered to die in another's stead, and Nitobe defends it, calling the boy a conscious and willing victim. The principal type of criticism here is ground conflict — he holds that the interests of a house and of its members are one and indivisible, and by that the child's standing as an independent end is cancelled.

And the volume closes by drawing out one line the material forces: the line between preserving the carrier and mere acquiescence lies not in the magnitude of the cost but in whether, after the concession, the standing as a subject has been handed over.

1. To Court Death Is Cowardice

The commonest impression of bushido is seeking death. Nitobe denies this explicitly, and his denial is not an incidental qualification but a recurring claim. At the close of the chapter on suicide: still, for a true samurai to hasten death or to court it, was alike cowardice.

And he gives a specimen. A warrior defeated in battle after battle, chased from plain to hill and from bush to cavern, hungry and alone in the hollow of a tree, his sword blunt, his bow broken, his arrows spent — he held death to be cowardice, and with a fortitude approaching a Christian martyr's composed an extempore verse: come, oh come, ye dread of dreads, pile ye up on my shoulders' strength; that I may not lack the strength to test how much I can endure.

In the situation with the strongest reasons for self-slaughter, this man held self-slaughter to be cowardice.

2. A Dog's Death, and to Dare to Live

From the chapter on courage: death for a cause unworthy of dying for, was called a dog's death. He quotes the Prince of Mito: to rush into the thick of battle and to be slain in it is easy enough, and the merest churl is equal to the task; but it is true courage to live when it is right to live, and to die only when it is right to die. And he distinguishes explicitly: to run all kinds of hazards, to place oneself in jeopardy, to rush into the jaws of death, are often identified with valour, and in the profession of arms such rashness — what Shakespeare calls valour misbegotten — is unjustly applauded; but not so in the Precepts of Knighthood.

He quotes Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici, and says it is an exact English rendering of what their precepts taught over and over: it is a brave act of valour to contemn death; but where life is more terrible than death, it is then the truest valour to dare to live.

So the honour system Nitobe sets out explicitly rejects the courting of death and dying for what is unworthy, and places living when it is right to live among the marks of true courage. This overlaps closely in conclusion with SAE's prohibition on self-destruction, which holds that one may not complete a gesture by way of destroying the carrier of cultivation. The two criteria are aimed at the same class of act.

3. A Contrast That Must Be Supplied: Here He Is Not a Transmitter

The three items above read like the tradition's own account of itself. They are not. The most famous line of the Hagakure is: the way of the samurai is found in death. What follows it carries no qualification to the effect that this is not the courting of death. On the contrary, it says that at the moment of choosing between two courses one should settle quickly upon the side of death, and act with a mind so settled.

And it then raises the most natural objection itself — if one dies without accomplishing the aim, is that not a dog's death? — and dismisses it. The reason: in a real predicament one cannot foresee which course will attain the aim; and since men naturally incline toward living, one's reasoning will attach itself to the side of preserving life. That being so, settling the mind on the side of death is what keeps one from being led by that inclination. So on one and the same term the two run in opposite directions.

In this one place, on the question of living and dying, what Nitobe sets out runs contrary to the direction of the Hagakure's opening passage, and he does not note the difference. The reason for the narrowing must be given: to write that he made a systematic revision would exceed the material — this volume examined a single opening passage, made no survey of the whole book, and examined none of the tradition's other literature. From one contrary direction, systematic does not follow. So this claims one divergence, not a programme of revision — and its function is to limit the object of the criticism below to Nitobe's own claim at that place, not to the tradition.

Use of “a dog's death”

NitobeA positive criterion

4. The Reasons Differ

His argument hangs on honour. Courting death is cowardice not because life has value in itself but because one who courts death is buying the appearance of honour with an easy act — rushing into battle to be killed is something the merest churl is equal to, so it proves nothing. He connects this to Mencius: Heaven, when it is about to confer a great office, first exercises the mind with suffering and the sinews with toil — so endurance is part of the office. And then the criterion: true honour lies in fulfilling Heaven's decree, and no death incurred in so doing is ignominious; whereas death to avoid what Heaven has in store is cowardly indeed. So his criterion is: does this death serve that decree.

SAE's reason is different, and stating it requires avoiding the language of ownership. This volume does not write that carrier does not belong wholly to him. Such a formulation describes a person as a thing partly owned by others, and that is precisely the grammar this series exists to refuse: a person who can be partly owned by others is not an end but property — and to argue you may not cancel yourself in the language of property leaves the door open, once the argument succeeds, to others' right of disposal over him.

Relation-and-responsibility language instead: a subject's termination terminates not only his own unfolding but the relations and undertakings that unfold on condition of him; he bears responsibility toward those relations, and the other parties to those relations do not thereby hold rights over him. The difference is real: ownership language permits the step since it does not belong to you alone, the community may dispose of you. Responsibility language does not permit it — a responsibility cannot be turned round into another's right of disposal.

And the difference in range: Nitobe's criterion ceases to block where honour genuinely requires death; SAE's still blocks. On his criterion, whether a death is admissible depends on whether it serves the decree — so where the decree does require death, his criterion not only fails to block, it pushes. And his own examples are of that kind: seppuku as an institution is the route by which a samurai could expiate crimes, apologise for errors, escape disgrace, redeem friends, or prove his sincerity, and in four of those five death is the way the office is discharged. SAE's does not vary with that condition: he still bears responsibility toward those relations that unfold on condition of him, and that does not change because honour requires something. The practical significance: Nitobe blocks dying for the appearance of honour, and does not block dying for its substance — and the latter is the class that actually occurs within this system.

5. Two Things He Criticises Himself

His criticism of giri — obligation — is severe: giri thus understood is a severe taskmaster, with a birch-rod in his hand to make sluggards perform their part. It is a secondary power in ethics… owing to this artificiality, giri degenerated in time into a vague sense of propriety called up to explain this and sanction that — as, for example, why a mother must, if need be, sacrifice all her other children in order to save the first-born; or why a daughter must sell her chastity to get funds to pay for the father's dissipation. Starting as right reason, giri has, in my mind, often stooped to casuistry. It has even degenerated into cowardly fear of censure.

This criticism is consistent with SAE's position: a norm that replaces the subject's judgement with an external sense of propriety will be used to argue for anything. And the reasons are close. His turns on giri's artificiality and its being secondary — it does not grow out of the person but is a substitute set up by the social structure so that obligations can be enforced where affection is absent. SAE would put it more specifically: it moves the position of judgement from the subject to an external standard of propriety, and once moved, anyone can occupy it. The two examples he gives both use one person as a means to another, and both appear in the form of this is how it ought to be.

The second is shame, and here SAE agrees with reservation. He describes it as the principal lever of a child's moral education — you will be laughed at, do you not feel ashamed? were the last appeals to correct behaviour on the part of a youthful delinquent — and his own evaluation is positive: the sense of shame seems to me the earliest indication of the moral consciousness of our race. This volume does not dispute whether it is the earliest; that is an empirical judgement about developmental order. What is to be pointed out is its position. Shame is a reaction to being seen — its occurrence requires an observer, whether physically present, imagined, or an internalised communal gaze. So in a normative system whose principal lever is shame, the standard lies outside the subject, and the subject's task is to conform to it.

And Theorem Four requires the opposite direction: that a subject cannot-not be questioned, and that questioning requires the subject to be able to answer — able to say I think that standard is wrong. Shame does not supply that position: the correct response to shame is correction, not rebuttal. One thing must be acknowledged: he sees part of this problem himself, writing that giri has even degenerated into cowardly fear of censure — which is what the shame lever looks like when it runs out of control. He criticised the loss of control; he did not criticise the lever.

6. The One Place of Divergence: the Story

In the chapter on loyalty, Nitobe says himself that he will give an example that may possibly shock some readers. Sugawara no Michizane was exiled; his political enemies meant to root out his line, and found that his young son was hidden in a village school kept by an old retainer, Genzō. The order came down: on such a day, produce the head of the young criminal. The first thing that occurred to Genzō was to find a substitute. He went through the school register, he scrutinised every boy who entered the classroom; not one resembled the child he was protecting. Then a new pupil arrived — a comely boy of the same age as his lord's son, brought by a mother of noble bearing.

Nitobe inserts a sentence here, and it is the most consequential in the passage: the mother and the boy himself were equally conscious of the resemblance between the young lord and his young servant. In the privacy of home both had laid themselves upon the altar: the one his life — the other her heart, yet without sign to the outer world. Unaware of what had passed between them, the teacher himself proposed the substitute. On the appointed day, the officer come to verify the head — the boy's own father — took up the dreadful object, calmly examined feature after feature, and in a composed, businesslike tone pronounced it genuine. That evening, crossing his own threshold, he said to his wife: rejoice, my wife, our darling son has proved of service to his lord.

7. His Defence

Nitobe anticipates the reader's reaction and answers it: “what a cruel story!” I hear my readers exclaim — “parents deliberately sacrificing their own innocent child to save the life of another man's.” But this child was a conscious and willing victim: it is a story of vicarious death — as significant as, and not more revolting than, the story of Abraham's intended sacrifice of Isaac. In both cases it was obedience to the call of duty, utter submission to the command of a higher voice… but I abstain from preaching.

And immediately after, the structural account he gives: individualism in the West, in recognising the separate interests of father and son, husband and wife, necessarily brings into strong relief the duties owed by one to the other; but Bushido held that the interest of the family and of the members thereof is intact — one and inseparable.

This place touches the ground of humanity is an end, and must be criticised. The point of contact is unmistakable: a child is handed over as a substitute for another child, and the defence takes the form of he was willing.

8. The Principal Criticism Is Ground Conflict

A more convenient line of criticism must be excluded first: that he violates the criteria he set down above — internal failure. Two common arguments for that line do not hold. The first says that judging whether a thing is worth dying for requires the dier's own judgement; the second says the tree-hollow warrior was required to endure, so why not this child. Both assume that worth dying for is settled by individual weighing. In Nitobe's system it is not. What settles it is duty — given externally by the position a person occupies. The tree-hollow warrior's duty required him to live, his task being unfinished; Genzō's substitute's duty required him to die, his position making him able to serve as a substitute. Within that system the two are consistent, not in conflict — those are not two applications of one criterion, but two conclusions of one criterion at two different positions.

The principal criticism: what Nitobe maintains here is that the interests of a house and of its members are one and indivisible. By that, the child's standing as an independent end is cancelled. He states it plainly himself, and this is a straightforward ground conflict; there is no need to pretend that he has given and then violated a unified criterion of living and dying. SAE's ground requires that each person have a position as an end which cannot be merged. A system that merges members' interests into the whole of the house cancels exactly that position. And in this particular arrangement, the result of the cancellation is: the whole of that child's function within it is that his face resembled another child's.

This place needs no demonstration that he contradicts himself, and none should be sought. Where a text touches the ground, one says so without detour; the convenience of the detour is false — if the other party's system is in fact internally coherent, the detour is a construction, and a reader who checks will disbelieve both it and everything else.

9. A Word Carrying More Than His Own Account Can Support

This criticism is not internal failure; it lies on the argument axis. He records himself how the lever of shame operates on children — you will be laughed at, this will disgrace you, do you not feel ashamed? are the last appeals to correct a youthful delinquent — and calls shame the earliest indication of moral consciousness. And he criticises giri for degenerating into cowardly fear of censure. And the word he uses to defend this sacrifice is a conscious and willing victim.

This is not he contradicts himself — he never maintained that willing means free of moral formation, so he violates no claim of his own. It is that the weight the word carries here cannot be supported by his own account of moral formation. He knows better than anyone how strong that lever is; he devotes a passage to how it works on children. And at the place where it most needs saying what this child's willingness amounts to, he does not bring that knowledge to bear. This is a criticism of the sufficiency of an argument, not of the consistency of a system. Its force is less than internal failure would be, but it is real: an argument has used a concept it has itself already weakened.

10. What SAE Says Here, and the Abraham Analogy

SAE's position can be stated in one sentence, and it introduces nothing new: willing cannot make a person a means and no longer an end. The formulation does not say you may not use a person as a means without consent. It says you may not use a person merely as a means. Consent changes one aspect of the matter; it does not change that person's position within the arrangement — and the whole of his function within this arrangement is that his face resembles another child's.

And the Abraham analogy is a second defect on the argument axis: evidence pointing the other way. Nitobe says the two are as significant as, and not more revolting than, one another. But the story ends with an angel staying the knife. The point of that story is precisely that the sacrifice did not take place. In Genzō's story the blade fell, the head was verified, and the father went home and said what he said. Nitobe cited a counterexample in his own support. This is neither internal failure nor ground conflict — he violates no claim of his own, and at this step he cancels no one's standing as an end. It is that the evidence he brought points the other way. The shape the two defects share: the material an argument uses stands, under its user's own handling, on the opposite side.

11. One Thing That Must Be Said

The criticism here may not be read as a verdict on bushido as a whole, nor as a comparison of cultures. Reason one: Nitobe himself supplies elsewhere the criteria SAE agrees with, and by the earlier finding those criteria are his own at that point rather than the tradition's transmission. So this is not how that system of theirs is but this author's claim at this place conflicts with SAE's ground.

Reason two: delivering another's child to die is not the property of any one culture. Nitobe himself cites Abraham. And any system that places something — a house, a lord, a cause, a nation — above its members and declares that the interest is one and inseparable will produce the same act somewhere.

Reason three, and the most important: what is criticised here is not those parents, and not that child. It is the sentence of defence. Those parents did what they did, at a cost beyond estimation; and Nitobe in 1899 wrote for it this child was a conscious and willing victim — and it is that sentence which turns a tragedy into a model that can be recommended.

12. A Line the Material Forces

Between preserving the carrier and mere acquiescence, the line lies not in the magnitude of the cost but in whether, after the concession, the standing as a subject has been handed over. This does not belong in a closing list of loose ends, for a reason: the prohibition on self-destruction has a direction in which it is easily misused — if preserving the carrier is a precept, then any surrender, any compromise, any concession can invoke it in its own defence. And this volume's material forces the line out, because the whole force of Nitobe's system is directed against exactly that misuse: what he means to block is the man who is always calculating whether he can survive, and such a man can indeed accomplish nothing.

The line: preserving the carrier is not fighting this time, because fighting would cost this community its capacity to go on cultivating — after not fighting it is still there, its cultivation still continuing, only in a changed form. Mere acquiescence is not fighting this time, in exchange for this community's accepting the position of a thing disposed of — it is still alive, but as a self-unfolding subject it is no longer there. The line does not lie in the magnitude of the cost: a community that has accepted extremely humiliating terms but kept its capacity to go on deciding its own direction is preserving the carrier; a community whose terms were not severe but which is thereafter directed by others is acquiescing, even if its losses were smaller.

This line holds up against a case of very great cost. Take Gandhian bearing: participants are arrested, beaten, dispossessed — the cost is not small — and what they surrender is bodily liberty, not the position from which they decide their own direction; the movement continues, and its direction is still set by the participants. On this line, that falls on the side of preserving the carrier. Set the line at magnitude of cost and that case cannot be decided; set it at has the standing as a subject been handed over and it decides cleanly. Whether to feed this back into the treatise, this volume does not answer — but as it stands the prohibition does not contain it, and without it the prohibition can be invoked to justify any concession whatever.

13. Left Unresolved in This Volume

The shame lever places the standard outside the subject, contrary to the direction Theorem Four requires. But SAE offers no replacement. How a community is to transmit norms to children without using shame is not answered here, and the question is not rhetorical — shame is universally used because it works. A related observation is kept: the spiritual cohesion demanded by the theorists of total war and the lever of shame treated here point in the same direction — conformity, not judgement. The difference is only of scale: shame operates within a family and a village, total war across an entire nation.

What willing amounts to in a child raised under the lever of shame raises a more general question: under what conditions does willing count? And the question is equally sharp for SAE — Theorem One's gate of genuine rising depends on the other party's actually wanting to resist, and that too is a judgement about willingness. Not answered here.

And the finding that Nitobe is a reviser rather than a transmitter rests on the direction of argument in a single opening passage, with no survey of the whole book. Its scope is confined to the question of living and dying, and may not be generalised to Nitobe revised bushido as a whole.

What This Is

This is not a ninth volume. It is the reckoning after the eight. Each volume treats one object — Kant; Clausewitz and On Protracted War; four mechanisms of recoil upon the user; Laozi, the Sima Fa and the Mozi; the just war tradition and Rousseau; Sunzi; Gandhi; Nitobe. What each yields is written in that volume and is not repeated here.

What this note answers is a different question: after running those eight, what does SAE have in hand that it did not have before. The answer is not we are better than they are. It is a shape — where SAE agrees with others for a different reason, where it draws its line earlier or later, where it must criticise, and where it has nothing to say.

What this series actually delivers is a set of things that need never have been said, and had to be said because they were said in front of someone else. Not one of them was learned from those others. Every one was forced out by their position.

VolumeObject

IIClausewitz and On Protracted War: authorisation by external purpose
IIIFour mechanisms by which a means reworks the hand that holds it
IVLaozi, the Sima Fa, the Mozi: four types of permission
VThe just war tradition and Rousseau: the adjudicating position

1. The Criterion Has No Authoriser

Clausewitz and On Protracted War give constraints sharing one form: war is authorised by an external political purpose and is therefore constrained by it. And that form has a shared limit — it cannot restrain the authoriser itself: a political purpose may expand in the course of things, and war may not exceed the purpose still holds. Only after setting them side by side did SAE have to say that it is not that shape.

Theorem Two draws no authorisation from an external purpose. Its criterion comes from cultivation, and cultivation cannot authorise its own cancellation — a criterion demanding the cancellation of a subject's unfolding cancels the condition of its own standing. From this follows an operating discipline for SAE itself: the criterion may not be hung on any particular good thing. The security of the state, the freedom of the republic, the liberation of a people — hang it there and you have an authoriser; have an authoriser and you have something it cannot restrain.

And this is not a cost. The criterion and the reason for mobilisation need not be the same thing: a particular good may mobilise; what it may not do is acquire, on its own strength alone, the standing to begin a war, to enlarge one, or to be exempt from review.

2. The Criterion on Means Has a Class of Blind Spot

Kant, Arendt, Machiavelli and SAE each supply one mechanism for a means reworks the party that wields it, and the four do not contain one another. What setting them side by side reveals is a specific blind spot: §12 binds the disqualification of deception to the information gap, so an arrangement conducted openly, with the executor fully informed, in which a person's standing as an end is nonetheless cancelled, draws no verdict from it.

There is a ready specimen of that blind spot: the substitution recorded by Nitobe — the parents knew, the boy knew, the teacher knew, and the officer who verified the head was the boy's own father. Everyone was informed, and the child's standing was nonetheless cancelled.

From this a gate is forced out: whether a means reworks its user, and whether an arrangement cancels a particular person, are two different questions, and a screen for either cannot substitute for the other.

3. Proportionality Blocks What the Bridge Clause Does Not

The bridge clause constraining means asks whether the road out is still there after the fighting, and needs no scale; proportionality asks how heavy the blow was, and needs a weigher. The two intersect; neither contains the other.

The bridge clause blocks what proportionality does not: a belligerent may sincerely hold its end to be of infinite value, but it cannot sincerely hold that a means which forecloses the other's possibility of reorganisation has not foreclosed it. And proportionality blocks what the bridge clause does not: an action that forecloses nothing yet is grossly disproportionate to its aim. SAE has a gap here, and the gap cannot be waved off with we do not make judgements of magnitude.

4. Theorem One's Threshold Depends on Execution-Layer Knowledge

Theorem One's threshold includes attacking-the-plan and breaking-alliances exhausted, and determining whether that is satisfied requires knowing what options they comprise and under what conditions each works — which is precisely the execution-layer knowledge SAE places outside its range.

A layer of principle may declare that it does not do the execution layer. It may not declare that it does not depend on one. And the practical consequence is not abstract: an agent who does not know what methods those two comprise will conclude there is no road while roads remain — and preventing exactly that is what Theorem One is for.

5. The Firewall Does Not Follow Directly from the Ground

Kant and SAE share a ground, and give different answers on whether a defeated state may be made to change its constitution: he permits it — limited to a constitution unfavourable by its nature to war, and with the people not losing its original right to constitute a commonwealth — and SAE's §18 does not. What this reveals is that the same ground does not automatically yield the same line.

Principle transfers; conclusions do not automatically cover. The ground confers the standing to ask across faces of relation; between the ground and a determinate line on some particular face there is a further stretch of road. Kant's stretch runs through Recht, SAE's through cultivation — and SAE's has not been walked to the end: why does any external condition on constitutional character displace the subject of cultivation? That argument does not currently exist.

6. The Line Between Preserving the Carrier and Mere Acquiescence

The prohibition on self-destruction has a direction in which it is easily misused: if preserving the carrier is a precept, then any surrender or compromise can invoke it in its own defence. Nitobe's material forces the line out, because the whole force of his system is directed against exactly that misuse — what he means to block is the man who is always calculating whether he can survive.

The line lies not in the magnitude of the cost but in whether, after the concession, the standing as a subject has been handed over. A community that has accepted extremely humiliating terms but kept its capacity to go on deciding its own direction is preserving the carrier; a community whose terms were not severe but which is thereafter directed by others is acquiescing — even if its losses were smaller.

7. Philosophy and Execution Are Two Opposite Directions Along One Axis

Not two stages of one task. The boundary between them is not clear, while each direction is: one end subtracts conditions, asking under what conditions a thing holds; the other adds them, asking what to do at this moment. Philosophy can treat ideal conditions precisely because it does not bear the consequences; execution must treat real conditions precisely because it does. The former's exemption is its working condition, the latter's constraint is its working condition — neither a defect, and neither a virtue.

Each end has its own way of going too far: philosophy gone too far leaves a criterion still coherent and no longer about anything; execution gone too far leaves a decision still makeable and no longer under any constraint. From this, two prohibitions: philosophy may not legislate for execution; execution may not cancel a criterion by appeal to being on the spot — you were not there is a fact about judgement, not an argument about a criterion.

And one thing must be written down hard: the authority to decide, the standing of those bearing risk to speak and refuse, and the standing of outside critics to question, are three different kinds of standing. Standing to question does not lapse for want of having borne the same consequences — otherwise Theorem Four is void, since you were not there becomes a universal exemption from all questioning.

8. Divergences Must Be Booked Separately

The discipline a different thought is not written as a correction previously had a posture and no form. And the consequence of having no form is observable: one and the same divergence will slide, as the prose requires, toward whichever type most favours one's own side. Four types on the relation axis: not covered; cross-domain non-transferable; ground conflict; internal failure. One axis for argument: sufficient or not — subdivided into a missing premise, a concept bearing more than it can, a failed analogy, evidence pointing the other way, over-generalisation, and inferring does not exist from not found.

The point is that the two are not on the same level: a defect of argument can occur in ourselves, and the first four cannot. SAE is in ground conflict with SAE is a meaningless thing to say; SAE's argument at this step is insufficient is not. Internal failure carries the heaviest burden of proof: one must first show that the other party himself claimed some aim or criterion, then show that by his own lights something fails, and that the failure does not depend on any criterion of SAE's. If any of the three is missing, it may not be registered as internal failure.

And a ground conflict needs no detour. The temptation is real — he violates his own criterion sounds more objective than he conflicts with our ground, because the former does not require the reader to accept our ground first. But the bargain is false: if the other party's system is in fact internally coherent, the detour is a construction, and a reader who checks it will disbelieve both that passage and everything else.

9. Three Items Returned to the Treatise

These three lie outside what this series can supply. First, an addition to §3: philosophy and execution are not two stages of one task but two opposite directions along one axis. §3's present formulation — the lightness of philosophy and the weight borne by those who execute — is a posture, and it still places the two on one line of comparison, leaving the tacit implication that execution is philosophy at a discount.

Second, an addition to §19: the line between preserving the carrier and mere acquiescence. §19 as it stands does not contain it, and without it §19 can be invoked to justify any concession whatever.

Third, the re-argument of §12. The legitimacy of the four-rung hierarchy of means previously drew in part on the attribution that Sunzi had already drawn a comparable distinction, and that attribution is withdrawn — Attack by Stratagem ranks objects of attack, while all warfare is based on deception states a mode of operation set down as a general proposition about all warfare; the two axes are orthogonal and form no ranked sequence. And volumes three and seven still use that hierarchy. This series can point out the gap; it cannot fill it.

10. One Last Thing, About This Series Itself

A framework that requires cannot-not be questioned must be the first thing questioned. Each volume therefore states in its body its own domain, the evidential status of its sources, and what it does not claim: which proposition holds only over the passages examined; which is a proposition awaiting verification; which can record only nothing found and cannot issue a certificate; which step is interpretation rather than quotation; and where a primary source could not be obtained, so that the associated judgement has been reduced.

Not one of these is invisible from outside. Because a set of criteria that cannot strike itself is not to be trusted when it judges others.
